explanation: Keep the lowest earlier price and the best profit found so far. Each price can be the selling day; a zero profit represents making no trade.
timeComplexity: O(n) time for n prices. One scan updates the minimum price and best profit in constant time per day.
spaceComplexity: O(1) auxiliary space. Only low and best are retained.
attribution: Original EPI Practice C# implementation, reusing and refining the repository-authored Blind75 algorithm fixtures. Collection membership follows Crackr; no external solution service is used.
correctness: The running minimum is the cheapest price seen before or at the current selling day. Buying at that minimum maximizes profit for this selling day, and the stored best covers all processed selling days. Starting best at zero permits no transaction when every sale would lose money.
walkthrough: For prices [8,3,7,2,9], price 7 gives profit 4 after buying at 3. A later price 2 becomes the new minimum; selling at 9 then gives profit 7. Return 7.
edgeCases: The purchase must precede the sale.
A decreasing price sequence returns zero.
A one-day sequence permits no profitable trade.

timeComplexity: O(c^(d+1) + output size) upper bound for c candidates and d = target / smallest candidate. The recursion depth is at most d=floor(target/min(candidates)); each level tries c candidates. Copying successful paths contributes the total output length.
spaceComplexity: O(d) recursion and current-path space, excluding output. The active path and recursion stack each have at most d entries; saved solutions are output space.

walkthrough: For candidates [3,4,7] and target 10, choosing 3,3,4 completes one branch. Choosing 3,7 completes another. No other candidate multiset totals 10, so return [[3,3,4],[3,7]].

timeComplexity: O(n log n) time for n input intervals. The implementation sorts n+1 intervals, then merges them in one pass; it does not exploit the already-sorted input for a linear insertion.
spaceComplexity: O(n) auxiliary and output space. The combined sorted sequence and copied result rows each require O(n) storage.

correctness: After sorting by start, the output contains the union of all intervals processed so far. A new interval overlaps the final output interval exactly when its start does not exceed that interval’s end; extending the end preserves the union. Otherwise it starts a separated component. Including the new interval in this sweep yields the complete updated union.
walkthrough: Insert [2,7] into [[0,2],[6,8]]. Closed intervals [0,2] and [2,7] touch and merge to [0,7]. That range overlaps [6,8], so the final result is [[0,8]].
edgeCases: Input intervals are sorted, disjoint closed ranges.
Touching endpoints merge in this collection.
The new interval may bridge several original intervals.

explanation: Sort intervals by start. Merge each interval into the last result when their closed ranges touch or overlap; otherwise start a new result range.
timeComplexity: O(n log n) time for n intervals. Sorting n intervals dominates the linear merge scan.
spaceComplexity: O(n) auxiliary and output space. The sorted sequence and independent result rows each require O(n) storage.

correctness: Sort by the left endpoint so a later interval cannot overlap any completed output range except the last one. Merging overlapping or touching ranges preserves their union; starting a new range when separated preserves disjointness. The final output is therefore exactly the input union.

edgeCases: Intervals may arrive unsorted.
Nested intervals do not shorten an existing merged range.
Equal endpoints are included and merge when they touch.

explanation: Sort by finishing time and greedily retain each interval whose start is at least the last retained end. The earliest finish leaves the most room for future intervals.
timeComplexity: O(n log n) time for n intervals. Sorting by finish time costs O(n log(n+1)); the greedy scan then inspects each interval once.
spaceComplexity: O(n) auxiliary space for sorting. The sorted copy contains n interval records or references, with constant scan state.
attribution: Original EPI Practice C# implementation, reusing and refining the repository-authored Blind75 algorithm fixtures. Collection membership follows Crackr; no external solution service is used.
correctness: Among intervals available next, retaining one with the earliest finish leaves at least as much room for every later choice as retaining any other interval. Exchanging an optimal solution’s first choice with that earliest-finishing choice cannot reduce its size. Repeating this argument proves the greedy maximum retained set; removing the rest is minimal.
walkthrough: For [[0,3],[2,4],[4,6],[5,7]], retain [0,3], reject overlapping [2,4], retain [4,6], then reject overlapping [5,7]. Two intervals can remain, so remove 4-2=2.
edgeCases: Touching intervals are compatible because positive overlap is required.
Identical positive-length intervals cannot both be retained.
An empty input needs no removals.

explanation: Sort meetings by start and compare consecutive intervals. A meeting starting before the previous one ends requires a second room.
timeComplexity: O(n log n) time for n meetings. Sorting by start dominates the n-1 adjacent comparisons.
spaceComplexity: O(n) auxiliary space. A separate sorted sequence holds n interval records or references.
attribution: Original EPI Practice C# implementation, reusing and refining the repository-authored Blind75 algorithm fixtures. Collection membership follows Crackr; no external solution service is used.
correctness: After sorting by start, any overlap involves an adjacent conflicting pair: if a meeting starts before an earlier meeting ends, then the latest preceding start also witnesses some overlap when all preceding adjacent pairs were compatible. Checking each consecutive end/start boundary therefore detects exactly whether one person can attend all meetings.
walkthrough: For meetings [0,2],[2,5],[6,9], the second begins exactly when the first ends, and the third begins after the second ends. No positive-duration overlap exists, so return true.
edgeCases: An end time equal to the next start is allowed.
The input need not be sorted.
Empty or singleton schedules are always attendable.

spaceComplexity: O(n) auxiliary space. A separate sorted sequence holds n interval records or references.
attribution: Original repository-authored Blind75 Java algorithm, promoted from the validated correct fixtures. Collection membership follows Crackr; no external solution service is used.
correctness: After sorting by start, any overlap involves an adjacent conflicting pair: if a meeting starts before an earlier meeting ends, then the latest preceding start also witnesses some overlap when all preceding adjacent pairs were compatible. Checking each consecutive end/start boundary therefore detects exactly whether one person can attend all meetings.
walkthrough: For meetings [0,2],[2,5],[6,9], the second begins exactly when the first ends, and the third begins after the second ends. No positive-duration overlap exists, so return true.
edgeCases: An end time equal to the next start is allowed.
The input need not be sorted.
Empty or singleton schedules are always attendable.

explanation: Turn meetings into start and end events and sort them. Process ends before starts at equal times; the maximum active count is the number of rooms needed.
timeComplexity: O(n log n) time for n meetings. Two events per meeting are sorted, then each event changes the active count once.
spaceComplexity: O(n) auxiliary space. The event array holds 2n entries; the active and maximum counts are constant space.
attribution: Original EPI Practice C# implementation, reusing and refining the repository-authored Blind75 algorithm fixtures. Collection membership follows Crackr; no external solution service is used.
correctness: The sweep’s active count equals the number of meetings occupying rooms at the current event boundary. Processing ends before starts at the same time releases reusable rooms first. Any schedule needs at least the maximum simultaneous count, and assigning a free room whenever active decreases realizes that bound.
walkthrough: For [0,4],[1,3],[3,6],[6,8], two rooms are needed between times 1 and 3. At time 3 one meeting ends before another starts, so occupancy stays at two. At time 6 a room is released before reuse. Return 2.
edgeCases: Touching meetings can reuse a room.
The largest simultaneous count, not the total meeting count, determines the answer.
An empty schedule needs zero rooms.

explanation: XOR every index and every value, starting with n. Values present in both ranges cancel, leaving the missing member of 0 through n.
timeComplexity: O(n) time for n values. Each index and input value contributes one XOR in a single scan.
spaceComplexity: O(1) auxiliary space. Only the missing accumulator and loop index are retained.
attribution: Original EPI Practice C# implementation, reusing and refining the repository-authored Blind75 algorithm fixtures. Collection membership follows Crackr; no external solution service is used.
correctness: XOR is associative and each value XOR itself is zero. Every present member of 0..n appears once among the indices plus n and once among the array values, so it cancels. Only the missing member occurs once and remains.
walkthrough: For [4,0,1,3], n=4. XOR the full range {0,1,2,3,4} with the input values {4,0,1,3}. All shared values cancel, leaving 2.
edgeCases: The missing value may be zero or n.
Values are distinct and lie in 0..n.
Input order does not matter.

explanation: Sort the characters of both strings and compare the resulting sequences. Equal sorted sequences have exactly the same character multiplicities.
timeComplexity: O(a log a + b log b) time for string lengths a and b. Sorting both character sequences dominates their final equality comparison.
spaceComplexity: O(a + b) auxiliary space. Character buffers or sorted copies hold both strings.
attribution: Original EPI Practice C# implementation, reusing and refining the repository-authored Blind75 algorithm fixtures. Collection membership follows Crackr; no external solution service is used.
correctness: Sorting places equal characters together in a canonical order. Two strings produce the same sorted sequence exactly when every character has the same multiplicity, which is precisely the anagram condition.
walkthrough: Sort "cider" into "cdeir" and "cried" into "cdeir". The canonical sequences match, so return true.
edgeCases: Only lowercase English letters occur in this contract.
Different lengths cannot have equal multiplicities.
Repeated letters must have matching counts; two empty strings are anagrams.

explanation: Count each lowercase letter in both strings using Counter, then compare the frequency maps. Matching multiplicities are sufficient because order does not matter.
timeComplexity: O(a+b) time: count a and b characters, then compare at most 26 entries.
spaceComplexity: O(1) auxiliary space under the lowercase-English contract: each Counter has at most 26 keys.
attribution: Original repository-authored Blind75 Python algorithm, promoted from the validated correct fixtures. Collection membership follows Crackr; no external solution service is used.
correctness: For every letter, Counter records its number of occurrences. Equality of the two maps means every letter has equal multiplicity, which is exactly the anagram condition; any mismatch makes the strings non-anagrams.
walkthrough: For "cider" and "cried", each counter contains c:1,d:1,e:1,i:1,r:1. The maps match despite the different order, so return true.
edgeCases: Only lowercase English letters occur in this contract.
Different lengths cannot have equal multiplicities.
Repeated letters must have matching counts; two empty strings are anagrams.

explanation: Use the sorted characters of a word as its grouping key. Return every group, including singleton groups, as required by this Blind75 contract.
timeComplexity: O(N + S log(L + 1)) time for N words, total characters S and maximum word length L. Each word is sorted to form its key; summing O(length log(length+1)) over all words gives O(S log(L+1)), plus visiting N words and expected hash lookup costs.
spaceComplexity: O(N + S) grouping and key space, plus output references. Keys contain at most S characters and the groups retain N input occurrences.
attribution: Original EPI Practice C# implementation, reusing and refining the repository-authored Blind75 algorithm fixtures. Collection membership follows Crackr; no external solution service is used.
correctness: A sorted-character key is equal exactly for words with the same character multiset. Appending each original word to its key’s bucket therefore creates all anagram classes, with every input occurrence present once. Returning all buckets retains singleton classes as this contract requires.
walkthrough: For ["arc","rat","car","tar","owl"], keys acr,art,acr,art,low create groups ["arc","car"],["rat","tar"],["owl"]. Return all three groups, including the singleton owl.
edgeCases: Singleton groups are included, unlike the EPI variant.
Repeated identical words remain repeated entries.
Group order and word order within a group are unrestricted.

explanation: Prefix each string with its decimal character length and a colon. Decoding reads that length and consumes exactly that many characters, so delimiters and empty strings are unambiguous. No object or process state carries the data.
timeComplexity: O(S + k log(L + 2)) time for k strings, total characters S and maximum string length L. Each payload character and decimal length-prefix character is written and read a constant number of times.
spaceComplexity: O(S + k log(L + 2)) encoded/output space, including length prefixes for empty strings. The encoded string and decoded items include all S payload characters and k length prefixes.
attribution: Original EPI Practice C# implementation, reusing and refining the repository-authored Blind75 algorithm fixtures. Collection membership follows Crackr; no external solution service is used.
correctness: Each encoded item begins with a decimal length followed by a delimiter, so the decoder knows exactly how many subsequent characters belong to that item. Delimiters inside content are never interpreted as boundaries. Repeating this step uniquely reconstructs the complete list, including empty items, from the string alone.
walkthrough: For ["","x:y","4#\n"], item lengths are 0,3 and 3. Their encoded pieces are "0:","3:x:y" and a piece beginning "3:4#" followed by a newline. Decoding consumes those exact lengths and recovers the original three strings, including the empty one and newline. The example represents Encode followed by Decode on a fresh instance; expected is the recovered list, not the encoded wire string.
edgeCases: An empty list differs from a list containing an empty string.
Colons and digits inside content are ordinary characters.
The decoder runs independently and cannot rely on cached input objects.

explanation: Keep ASCII letters and digits, normalize letters to lowercase, and compare the filtered sequence with its reverse.

explanation: Maintain a window with distinct characters. When a character repeats, move the left edge past its previous position without moving it backward.
timeComplexity: O(n) expected time for n characters. The right boundary visits each character once; the last-occurrence lookup gives the new left boundary directly.
spaceComplexity: O(min(n, alphabet size)) auxiliary space. Last occurrences need one entry per represented character, never one entry per window.
attribution: Original EPI Practice C# implementation, reusing and refining the repository-authored Blind75 algorithm fixtures. Collection membership follows Crackr; no external solution service is used.
correctness: The window’s left boundary stays after the previous occurrence of each character in the window. Moving it to at least one past a repeated character restores distinctness without discarding any longer valid suffix ending here. Taking the largest such suffix length over every endpoint finds the global optimum.
walkthrough: For "dvdf", the second d at index 2 moves the left boundary from 0 to 1. The final window becomes "vdf", whose three characters are distinct. Return 3.
edgeCases: The answer counts a contiguous substring, not a subsequence.
The left boundary never moves backward.
An empty string returns zero.

explanation: Track a sliding window and its largest observed character frequency. Shrink when the window length minus that frequency exceeds k. The historical maximum safely bounds the longest achievable window.
timeComplexity: O(n) time for n uppercase letters. The right boundary advances n times and the left boundary at most n times.
spaceComplexity: O(1) auxiliary space for 26 counters. Counts cover only the fixed 26-letter alphabet; the window indices and historical maximum are scalars.
attribution: Original EPI Practice C# implementation, reusing and refining the repository-authored Blind75 algorithm fixtures. Collection membership follows Crackr; no external solution service is used.
correctness: With an exact frequency f, a length-w window needs w-f replacements. most never decreases: when it increases to f, the current character really occurs f times in the window. The loop retains width at most most+k, and width cannot grow while most is stale after shrinking: the previous width was already most+k. Consequently each newly recorded larger width is witnessed while the count supplying most is present, and is feasible. Stale counts may retain an infeasible window of an already-achieved width, but cannot inflate best. Finally, shrinking on w-most>k is safe because the true maximum frequency is at most most; such a window really is infeasible. Thus no optimal width is discarded.
walkthrough: For "AAABBC" with k=1, the window "AAAB" contains three As and one B, so one replacement creates four As. Extending it to "AAABB" would require two replacements. No later window is longer and feasible, so return 4.
edgeCases: k=0 reduces to the longest equal-character run.
The input alphabet is uppercase A through Z.
At most k replacements are allowed; unused replacements are permitted.

explanation: Count the characters still needed from t. Expand until all occurrences are covered, then shrink from the left while preserving coverage. Update only for strictly shorter windows to retain the earliest tie.
timeComplexity: O(s + t) time for string lengths s and t. Counting t is linear; each character of s enters and leaves the window at most once. Copying the final answer costs at most O(s).
spaceComplexity: O(1) counters for the fixed ASCII alphabet, plus the returned substring. The need table is bounded by the ASCII alphabet, with constant boundary and length state.
attribution: Original EPI Practice C# implementation, reusing and refining the repository-authored Blind75 algorithm fixtures. Collection membership follows Crackr; no external solution service is used.
correctness: The need counters track uncovered target occurrences after subtracting the current window’s characters. missing is zero exactly when every required occurrence is covered. For each right endpoint, shrinking until coverage would fail finds its shortest valid window. Comparing these candidates globally gives a minimum, and updating only when strictly shorter preserves the earliest tie. For ties, left boundaries only advance, so a later equal-length candidate cannot have an earlier start.
walkthrough: For s="xcaabz" and t="aab", coverage first requires both a characters and b. Removing leading x and c leaves "aab", already the target’s full length, so no shorter covering window exists. Return "aab".
edgeCases: Target multiplicities matter: two As require two occurrences.
The target is nonempty in this collection.
No covering window returns an empty string.
Equal-length optimal windows choose the earliest start.

explanation: Expand around every character and every gap between characters. Track the longest palindrome and choose the earliest starting index when lengths tie.
timeComplexity: O(n squared) time for n characters. There are 2n centers and at most n outward comparisons per center. Only the final substring is copied.
spaceComplexity: O(1) auxiliary space excluding the returned substring. Each expansion uses two indices and the best interval; no table of substrings is stored.
attribution: Original EPI Practice C# implementation, reusing and refining the repository-authored Blind75 algorithm fixtures. Collection membership follows Crackr; no external solution service is used.
correctness: Every palindrome has either one center character or one center gap. Expanding each such center enumerates exactly its palindromic radii until the next pair mismatches. The stored longest candidate therefore covers every possible palindrome; the start-index comparison implements the earliest tie rule.
walkthrough: For "qlevelz", expand around the middle v. Equal e characters yield "eve", then equal l characters yield "level". The surrounding q and z differ, so expansion stops at length 5. Return "level".
edgeCases: Both odd and even centers must be examined.
An empty string returns empty.
When several longest palindromes tie, choose the earliest start.

explanation: Push opening brackets on a stack. Each closing bracket must match the most recent opening bracket; the stack must be empty at the end.
timeComplexity: O(n) time for n brackets. Each bracket is pushed or matched/popped at most once.
spaceComplexity: O(n) auxiliary space. A prefix of n opening brackets requires n stack entries.
attribution: Original EPI Practice C# implementation, reusing and refining the repository-authored Blind75 algorithm fixtures. Collection membership follows Crackr; no external solution service is used.
correctness: The stack lists precisely the unmatched opening brackets in nesting order. A closing bracket is valid exactly when it matches the most recent unmatched opening; popping preserves that invariant. The entire sequence is valid only when every close matches and the stack ends empty.
walkthrough: For "{[()]()}", push {, [, (. The next ) and ] remove their matching tops. A later () pair also cancels, and the final } removes the initial {. The empty stack proves true.
edgeCases: A closing bracket cannot appear before its matching opening.
Nested pairs must close in reverse opening order.
An empty bracket string is valid.

explanation: Transpose the square matrix across its main diagonal, then reverse every row. Together these operations rotate values clockwise while preserving the original matrix and row objects.
timeComplexity: O(n squared) time for an n by n matrix. Transposition swaps each off-diagonal pair once; reversing all rows touches n squared entries.
spaceComplexity: O(1) auxiliary space. Swapping values requires only constant temporary state.
attribution: Original EPI Practice C# implementation, reusing and refining the repository-authored Blind75 algorithm fixtures. Collection membership follows Crackr; no external solution service is used.
correctness: Transposition maps each original cell (r,c) to (c,r), and reversing each row then maps it to (c,n-1-r). That is exactly the clockwise quarter-turn coordinate transformation. Only values are swapped, so the original matrix and row objects remain the same.
walkthrough: For [[2,5],[7,9]], transposition produces [[2,7],[5,9]]. Reversing both rows yields [[7,2],[9,5]], the clockwise rotation. The judge checks the changed original matrix rather than a replacement object. The callable returns no value; expected records the original matrix after mutation, and the harness additionally checks row identity.
edgeCases: The input matrix must be square.
A one-cell matrix is unchanged.
The original row objects must be preserved.

explanation: Maintain the unvisited top, bottom, left, and right boundaries. Consume each outside edge in clockwise order, checking boundaries before the final two edges.
timeComplexity: O(rows times columns) time. Each entry belongs to exactly one consumed boundary and is emitted once.
spaceComplexity: O(1) auxiliary space excluding output. Four boundaries and loop indices suffice; the result stores rows times columns values.
attribution: Original EPI Practice C# implementation, reusing and refining the repository-authored Blind75 algorithm fixtures. Collection membership follows Crackr; no external solution service is used.
correctness: The four boundaries enclose exactly the unvisited rectangle. Reading one outside edge visits each of its cells once, then moving that boundary inward removes exactly those visited cells. Guarding the final bottom and left edges prevents revisiting a single remaining row or column.
walkthrough: For [[2,4,6],[8,10,12]], read the top edge 2,4,6, then the right edge 12. The remaining bottom edge contributes 10,8 from right to left. Return [2,4,6,12,10,8].

A single row is emitted once from left to right.
A single column is emitted once from top to bottom.

explanation: Compare the middle value with the right endpoint. If it is larger, the minimum lies to the right; otherwise the middle remains a possible minimum.
timeComplexity: O(log n) time for n distinct values. Every comparison discards approximately half of the remaining candidate indices.
spaceComplexity: O(1) auxiliary space. The left, right, and middle indices are the only search state.
attribution: Original EPI Practice C# implementation, reusing and refining the repository-authored Blind75 algorithm fixtures. Collection membership follows Crackr; no external solution service is used.
correctness: The minimum remains inside the current closed search interval. If nums[mid] exceeds the right endpoint, the rotation break and minimum lie strictly to the right of mid; otherwise mid may itself be the minimum and the interval can end there. Each update preserves the invariant until one candidate remains.
walkthrough: For [11,14,2,5,8], the middle value 2 is no greater than the right value 8, so keep the left portion including 2. Comparing 14 with that endpoint then discards the part before 2. Return the minimum value 2.

An unrotated array has its minimum at index zero.
One value is already the answer.

explanation: Advance one pointer by one link and another by two. They meet inside a cycle; reaching a null fast pointer proves that the list terminates.
timeComplexity: O(n) time for n reachable nodes. Before entering a cycle the pointers take O(n) steps; inside it the relative position closes within one cycle length.

correctness: If the list terminates, the fast pointer reaches null. If a cycle exists, both pointers eventually enter it and their relative position advances by one cycle position per step, so they must meet. Thus reference equality of the pointers detects a cycle without changing the list.

The setup index is supplied to the judge, not to HasCycle. The extra serialized pos is harness setup, not a callable argument; expected is the returned boolean and the harness checks links and values remain unchanged.

spaceComplexity: O(n + h) auxiliary space for positions and recursion, plus the output tree. The position map stores n entries and recursion retains h interval frames; new nodes form the output.

explanation: Compute each subtree's best downward gain, discarding negative gains. At each node also consider joining the best left and right gains through that node, while returning only one branch to its parent.

spaceComplexity: O(h) recursion space for tree height h. The active recursive path has at most h frames; no paths are copied.

correctness: A downward path returned to a parent can include at most one child branch, so the recursive gain keeps the better nonnegative child gain. A complete path whose highest node is the current node may use both child gains. Considering that complete path at every node covers every possible nonempty simple tree path.
walkthrough: For [-5,4,7,2,3,null,6], the left gain into root -5 is 4+3=7 and the right gain is 7+6=13. Joining them through the root yields 7-5+13=15, realized by 3→4→-5→7→6. Return 15.

The path is nonempty, so an all-negative tree returns its largest node value.
Negative child gains are excluded instead of reducing a path.

explanation: Move left when both target values are smaller and right when both are larger. The first split, including a target node itself, is their lowest common ancestor and is returned by original identity.
timeComplexity: O(h) time for tree height h. Each iteration descends one level, stopping no later than tree height h.
spaceComplexity: O(1) auxiliary space. Only a moving root reference and the two target values are retained.

correctness: When both target keys lie below the current key, both targets and their LCA lie in its left subtree; the analogous rule holds on the right. explanation: Iterate the tree in inorder using an explicit stack, then require each value to be strictly smaller than the next. Strict comparison rejects duplicate keys.
timeComplexity: O(n) time for n nodes. Inorder visits each node once and the adjacent-value comparison scans the resulting array once.
spaceComplexity: O(n + h) auxiliary space for the materialized values and traversal stack. The materialized n values coexist with a traversal stack of at most h nodes.
attribution: Original EPI Practice C# implementation, reusing and refining the repository-authored Blind75 algorithm fixtures. Collection membership follows Crackr; no external solution service is used.
correctness: For any binary tree, the strict BST property is equivalent to strictly increasing inorder values. Inorder places all left descendants before their ancestor and all right descendants after it. Any nonincreasing adjacent pair proves an ordering violation; if every pair increases, every subtree has the required global ordering.
walkthrough: For [7,3,10,1,8], inorder values are [1,3,8,7,10]. The decrease from 8 to 7 shows that 8 lies incorrectly inside the root’s left subtree. Return false, even though 8 exceeds its immediate parent 3.
edgeCases: Duplicate keys are invalid in this strict BST contract.
An empty tree is valid.
Checking only direct parent-child comparisons misses ancestor violations.

explanation: Recursively materialize inorder as left-subtree values, current value, and right-subtree values. Require every adjacent pair in that complete array to be strictly increasing. The recursive array construction may repeatedly copy values.
timeComplexity: O(n squared) worst-case time: recursive inorder concatenation copies subtree values repeatedly along a skew tree; the final comparison or indexed lookup adds at most O(n).
spaceComplexity: O(n+h) live auxiliary values and recursion frames for n nodes and height h. Completed sibling results and partial inorder arrays together hold O(n) values; cumulative allocation/copying can be quadratic.

explanation: Iterate inorder with an explicit stack and stop at the kth value. BST inorder visits keys in sorted order.
timeComplexity: O(h + k) time for height h and rank k. The iterator descends at most h levels before and during its first k yields; each visited node is pushed and popped once.
spaceComplexity: O(h) auxiliary stack space. The lazy traversal stores at most h ancestor references and stops without materializing all values.
attribution: Original EPI Practice C# implementation, reusing and refining the repository-authored Blind75 algorithm fixtures. Collection membership follows Crackr; no external solution service is used.
correctness: Inorder traversal visits strict BST keys in increasing order. The explicit stack simulates that traversal, so the kth removed node is exactly the kth smallest key. Stopping there cannot skip any smaller key and avoids visiting unnecessary later nodes.

edgeCases: k is 1-based and lies within the node count.
A leftmost key answers k=1.
The explicit stack uses tree height rather than a copied tree.

explanation: Store one character per trie edge and mark terminal nodes. Insertion creates missing edges. Exact search requires a terminal marker. Prefix search requires a matching path and at least one stored word, so the empty prefix is false before any insertion, as this collection specifies.
timeComplexity: O(L) expected time per operation for word or prefix length L. Following or creating a path performs one expected constant-time child lookup per character.
spaceComplexity: O(T) stored trie nodes across all insertions; O(1) extra per search. One node is created per new prefix; a search holds only its current node reference.
attribution: Original EPI Practice C# implementation, reusing and refining the repository-authored Blind75 algorithm fixtures. Collection membership follows Crackr; no external solution service is used.
correctness: Every trie path spells exactly its edge characters, and a terminal marker denotes an inserted complete word. Insertion creates only the needed path and marks its endpoint. Exact search checks the terminal marker, while prefix search checks a path and the collection’s nonempty-word-set condition. Those rules distinguish an inserted word from a mere prefix.

Insert "mi", after which search("mi") is true. Query results are [false,true,false,true]. The arrays describe calls on one instance in order; expected contains only Search/StartsWith boolean results, omitting Insert returns.
edgeCases: Prefix search and exact search are different operations.
Reinserting the same word does not duplicate it.

spaceComplexity: O(S+W) stored content/references for W distinct words of total length S; prefix scanning itself needs constant extra state. JavaScript spreads the set into an O(W) temporary array for each prefix query.

explanation: Map every original node to its new copy before visiting its neighbors. This breaks recursive cycles and preserves adjacency while sharing no original graph nodes.
timeComplexity: O(V + E) expected time for reachable vertices V and directed adjacency entries E. The identity map processes each reachable vertex once and translates every adjacency entry once.
spaceComplexity: O(V) map/recursion space, plus O(V + E) cloned output. The map and recursion have at most V entries/frames; cloned vertices and edges are output space.
attribution: Original EPI Practice C# implementation, reusing and refining the repository-authored Blind75 algorithm fixtures. Collection membership follows Crackr; no external solution service is used.
correctness: The identity map creates one new vertex per original vertex before traversing its neighbors, so cycles cannot cause repeated cloning. Every original adjacency entry is translated through that map, preserving connectivity and sharing. All returned vertices are newly allocated and no original value or edge is modified.
walkthrough: For adjacency [[2],[1,3],[2]], allocate copies of vertices 1,2 and 3. The copied edges are 1↔2 and 2↔3, so the cloned adjacency is again [[2],[1,3],[2]], but every vertex is a different object from its original. Expected is serialized adjacency of the returned clone; the harness separately checks fresh nodes and preservation of the original graph.
edgeCases: An empty graph clones to null.
A single isolated vertex still needs a new object.
Returning the original graph fails even when its adjacency looks correct.

explanation: Flood inland from each ocean's boundary, traversing to equal or greater heights. These reversed paths identify cells that can drain to each ocean; return the intersection.
timeComplexity: O(rows times columns) time. Each of two reverse floods visits each cell at most once and examines four neighbors; the intersection scans the grid.
spaceComplexity: O(rows times columns) auxiliary and output space. Two visited grids and flood queues each have at most RC entries.
attribution: Original EPI Practice C# implementation, reusing and refining the repository-authored Blind75 algorithm fixtures. Collection membership follows Crackr; no external solution service is used.
correctness: A cell can drain to an ocean exactly when the ocean can reach it along reversed flow edges, from lower or equal height to higher or equal height. Flooding inland from every boundary touching each ocean therefore finds its complete drainage set. Intersecting the two sets returns exactly cells that can drain to both oceans.
walkthrough: For heights [[1,2],[4,3]], top-right (0,1) touches both the top and right boundaries; bottom-left (1,0) touches both left and bottom. Bottom-right (1,1) can also flow uphill in the reversed search from top-right, corresponding to real downhill drainage back to the Pacific. Return [[0,1],[1,0],[1,1]].
edgeCases: Equal-height flow is allowed.
A one-cell grid drains to both oceans.
Output coordinates are zero-based row,column pairs.

explanation: Build prerequisite-to-course edges and indegrees. Repeatedly remove a zero-indegree course and release its dependents. All courses are removable exactly when no directed cycle remains.
timeComplexity: O(V + E) time for V courses and E prerequisite pairs. Building adjacency and indegrees reads every edge; each vertex is removed once and each outgoing edge decremented once.
spaceComplexity: O(V + E) auxiliary space. Adjacency stores E edges, while indegrees and the ready queue each hold at most V entries.
attribution: Original EPI Practice C# implementation, reusing and refining the repository-authored Blind75 algorithm fixtures. Collection membership follows Crackr; no external solution service is used.
correctness: Indegree counts the unprocessed prerequisites of each course. A zero-indegree course can be completed, and removing it decrements exactly its dependents’ remaining prerequisite counts. A directed acyclic graph eventually releases every vertex. If processing stops early, every remaining course depends within the remainder, proving a cycle.
walkthrough: For four courses with prerequisites [1,0],[2,1],[3,1], begin with course 0. Finishing it releases course 1; finishing 1 releases both 2 and 3. All four courses are processed, so return true.
edgeCases: Isolated courses also need to be included in the processed count.
A self-dependency prevents completion.
No prerequisites makes every course immediately available.

explanation: Start with one disjoint set per vertex. For each edge, join different root sets and decrease the component count. Path halving shortens future root searches.
timeComplexity: O((V + E) log(V + 1)) amortized upper bound with path compression alone for V vertices and E edges. There are V initializations, two root searches per edge, and at most V-1 links. Path halving is present but union by rank is not, so the rank-plus-compression inverse-Ackermann claim is not used.
spaceComplexity: O(V) auxiliary space. The parent array has one entry per vertex; find is iterative.
attribution: Original EPI Practice C# implementation, reusing and refining the repository-authored Blind75 algorithm fixtures. Collection membership follows Crackr; no external solution service is used.
correctness: Initially each vertex forms its own connected component. An edge between different root sets merges exactly those two components and decreases the count once. An edge already inside one set changes no connectivity. After all edges, the disjoint sets coincide with graph components, including isolated vertices.
walkthrough: For n=6 and edges [0,1],[1,2],[3,4], merge 0,1,2 into one set and 3,4 into another. Vertex 5 stays isolated. The three sets {0,1,2},{3,4},{5} give result 3.
edgeCases: Isolated vertices count as components.
A repeated connection within an existing component must not decrease the count.
An empty graph with zero vertices has zero components.

timeComplexity: O(W + S + E + V log(V + 1)) expected time for W words, S input characters, V distinct characters and E distinct precedence edges. spaceComplexity: O(S + V + E) auxiliary space, including concatenated input characters. The graph stores V vertices and E distinct edges; this implementation also concatenates input characters.
attribution: Original EPI Practice C# implementation, reusing and refining the repository-authored Blind75 algorithm fixtures. Collection membership follows Crackr; no external solution service is used.
correctness: The first differing characters in adjacent sorted words give a necessary alphabet precedence edge; later characters cannot affect that comparison. A longer word before its own prefix is impossible. Any topological ordering of all seen characters satisfies every extracted comparison, while a cycle proves no alphabet can satisfy them all.
walkthrough: Words ["ca","cb","da","db"] require a before b and c before d. One valid character order is "abcd"; using it keeps all four words sorted. The algorithm’s smallest-ready-character rule returns that order.

A longer word preceding its own prefix returns an empty string.
Cycles return an empty string.
Several different alphabet orders may be valid.

explanation: Keep the ways to reach the previous two steps. Their sum gives the ways to reach the next step, corresponding to a final move of one or two steps.
timeComplexity: O(n) time for n steps. The loop computes one recurrence value per stair after the two base values.
spaceComplexity: O(1) auxiliary space. Only the preceding two counts and one temporary sum are retained.
attribution: Original EPI Practice C# implementation, reusing and refining the repository-authored Blind75 algorithm fixtures. Collection membership follows Crackr; no external solution service is used.
correctness: For a positive final step, every valid climb ends with either one step from n-1 or two steps from n-2, and these classes are disjoint. Their counts therefore add. Keeping the previous two recurrence values computes the same count without storing the whole table, including one empty climb at zero.
walkthrough: For n=5, the counts from stair 0 through stair 5 are 1,1,2,3,5,8. The final count is 5+3=8, representing all ordered sequences of one-step and two-step moves.
edgeCases: The public domain is 1≤n≤45.
The two base counts encode one way to reach stair 1 and the internal empty-prefix count.
Move order matters; the maximum promised n keeps the answer within signed 32-bit range.

explanation: For each house choose between skipping it and adding its value to the best total that excludes its neighbor. Retain only the previous two totals.
timeComplexity: O(n) time for n houses. One transition is evaluated per house.
spaceComplexity: O(1) auxiliary space. Only the optimal totals for the preceding two prefixes are retained.
attribution: Original EPI Practice C# implementation, reusing and refining the repository-authored Blind75 algorithm fixtures. Collection membership follows Crackr; no external solution service is used.
correctness: For each prefix, an optimal selection either skips the final house and keeps the preceding optimum, or takes it and adds its value to the optimum excluding its neighbor. These choices are exhaustive and legal. Taking their maximum maintains the prefix optimum using only two earlier totals.

A single house is handled by the same recurrence.
The input is a line; its first and last houses are not neighbors.

explanation: Track counts for the previous two prefixes. A nonzero final digit extends the previous prefix; a final pair from 10 through 26 extends the prefix before it. BigInteger preserves intermediate counts before the guaranteed int-sized final result.
timeComplexity: O(n) arithmetic operations for n digits; big-integer costs depend on intermediate count width. Each digit performs a constant number of count operations; counts have at most O(n) bits, so O(n squared) bit time is a safe upper bound.
spaceComplexity: Two BigInteger counts, using O(n) bits in the worst case. Only a constant number of arbitrary-precision counts coexist, each with O(n) bits.
attribution: Original EPI Practice C# implementation, reusing and refining the repository-authored Blind75 algorithm fixtures. Collection membership follows Crackr; no external solution service is used.
correctness: A decoding of each prefix ends with either a valid nonzero single digit or a valid pair from 10 through 26. Removing that final token gives a decoding of the preceding one- or two-shorter prefix. Those cases are disjoint and exhaustive, so adding their counts yields exactly all decodings. Arbitrary-precision intermediate counts prevent overflow before the final int result.

explanation: Track the previous two prefix counts as BigInt values. A nonzero final digit extends the previous prefix; a final pair from 10 through 26 extends the prefix before it. Convert the final guaranteed 32-bit result to Number.

Arbitrary-precision intermediate counts prevent overflow before the final int result.

explanation: Let dp[v] be the fewest coins for amount v. For each amount, try every coin as its last coin; retain an unreachable sentinel when no previous amount can form it.
timeComplexity: O(amount times c) time for c coin values. For each amount from 1 to amount, every one of c coins is tried as the final coin.
spaceComplexity: O(amount) auxiliary space. The table has amount+1 integer entries.
attribution: Original EPI Practice C# implementation, reusing and refining the repository-authored Blind75 algorithm fixtures. Collection membership follows Crackr; no external solution service is used.
correctness: For every amount v, the last coin of any solution leaves a smaller amount v-coin. Once those smaller optima are known, choosing one plus their minimum gives the optimum for v. If every predecessor is unreachable, v is unreachable too. Starting dp[0]=0 establishes the base case.
walkthrough: For coins [3,5] and amount 11, one valid construction is 3+3+5, using three coins. Neither one coin nor any two-coin sum from {3,5} equals 11. Return the minimum count 3.
edgeCases: Amount zero requires zero coins.
An unreachable positive amount returns -1.
Coin values are positive and distinct, and may be reused.

explanation: Retain both the largest and smallest products ending at the previous value. Multiplication by a negative number can swap their roles; compare both extensions with starting a new subarray.
timeComplexity: O(n) time for n values. Every value updates the minimum and maximum ending products in constant time.
spaceComplexity: O(1) auxiliary space. The recurrence itself needs only high, low, best, and two temporary products.
attribution: Original EPI Practice C# implementation, reusing and refining the repository-authored Blind75 algorithm fixtures. Collection membership follows Crackr; no external solution service is used.
correctness: Every subarray ending at the current position either starts there or extends one ending immediately before it. A negative multiplier can turn the previous minimum into the new maximum, so retaining both extrema covers all candidates. The greatest ending maximum across positions is the optimum over all nonempty subarrays.
walkthrough: For [-2,3,-4,0,2], products ending at 3 include -6 and 3. Multiplying the previous minimum -6 by -4 yields 24, from subarray [-2,3,-4]. Zero resets later products and the final 2 is smaller, so return 24.
edgeCases: The subarray is nonempty.
Zero can separate otherwise unrelated product ranges.
Both maximum and minimum ending products are needed for negative values.

explanation: Mark reachable prefix lengths, starting with zero. From each reachable position, advance by every dictionary word that matches there. The final position is reachable exactly when segmentation is possible.
timeComplexity: O((n + 1) times (D + 1)) time for string length n and total dictionary characters D, including an empty dictionary. For each reachable position, comparison with all words costs at most their total length D; even unreachable positions require the outer O(n) scan.
spaceComplexity: O(n) auxiliary space. The reachable-prefix table has n+1 booleans; comparisons do not store new substrings.
attribution: Original EPI Practice C# implementation, reusing and refining the repository-authored Blind75 algorithm fixtures. Collection membership follows Crackr; no external solution service is used.
correctness: Reachable[i] means the prefix ending before i can be segmented into dictionary words. From any reachable i, appending a matching word produces another valid segmented prefix. Conversely, every nonempty valid segmentation has a final dictionary word appended after a reachable earlier prefix, so these transitions discover every valid endpoint.
walkthrough: For "sunflower" and dictionary ["sun","flow","flower"], mark prefix length 3 after matching sun. From that position flower reaches the full string length 9. Therefore "sun"+"flower" is a valid segmentation and the result is true.
edgeCases: Dictionary words may be reused.
Dictionary entries are nonempty.
The full string must be covered, not merely a prefix.

explanation: Maintain the smallest possible tail for every subsequence length. Binary-search the first tail not smaller than each value and replace it, or append when all tails are smaller.
timeComplexity: O(n log(n + 1)) time for n values. Each of n values binary-searches at most n tails, then performs one update.
spaceComplexity: O(n) auxiliary space. There is one tail per attainable subsequence length, at most n.
attribution: Original EPI Practice C# implementation, reusing and refining the repository-authored Blind75 algorithm fixtures. Collection membership follows Crackr; no external solution service is used.
correctness: For each length, tails stores the smallest possible ending value of an increasing subsequence of that length. Replacing the first tail at least as large as a new value cannot invalidate shorter subsequences and improves future extension opportunities. Appending occurs exactly when a longer subsequence is possible, so the final tails length is optimal.
walkthrough: For [4,1,5,2,6,3,7], tails changes through [4],[1],[1,5],[1,2],[1,2,6],[1,2,3],[1,2,3,7]. Its final length is 4, witnessed by subsequence 1,2,3,7.
edgeCases: The subsequence need not be contiguous.
Equal values cannot extend a strictly increasing subsequence.
The tails array represents optimal ending values and need not itself reproduce an earlier input prefix.

correctness: Each operation n & (n-1) clears exactly the lowest set bit without changing any other set bit. Counting such operations until n becomes zero therefore counts all ones in the original unsigned 32-bit pattern.

edgeCases: The input is an unsigned 32-bit value carried in a long.

timeComplexity: O(n) time for results from 0 through n. Each result after zero takes one previously computed count and one low-bit addition.
spaceComplexity: O(1) auxiliary space excluding the O(n) output. The output array is the dynamic-programming table; loop indices need constant additional space.

correctness: The bits of i consist of the bits of i shifted right once, followed by its low bit. Therefore popcount(i)=popcount(i>>1)+(i&1). The shifted value is smaller, so its count is already available while filling the table in increasing order.

n=0 returns [0].
The recurrence needs no binary-string conversion.

explanation: Build the output with a list comprehension calling bit_count() independently for every integer from zero through n. This code uses the built-in population count rather than a recurrence between output entries.
timeComplexity: O(n+1) under the n≤100000 contract: every integer uses a bounded number of machine limbs, so each bit_count is constant time.
spaceComplexity: O(n+1) output space and O(1) auxiliary space for the comprehension’s current integer and count.
attribution: Original repository-authored Blind75 Python algorithm, promoted from the validated correct fixtures. Collection membership follows Crackr; no external solution service is used.
correctness: The comprehension visits each integer i in 0..n exactly once and places i.bit_count() at position i. Each value is the number of set bits in that nonnegative integer, so every required output entry is correct.
walkthrough: For n=6, the comprehension counts bits in 0,1,10,11,100,101,110. Those counts are 0,1,1,2,1,2,2, producing [0,1,1,2,1,2,2].

n=0 returns [0].
Every population count is computed independently; no previous result is read.

explanation: For every i, use the count for i shifted right by one and add its low bit. This reuses the previously computed count for half of i.
timeComplexity: O(n) time for results from 0 through n. Each result after zero takes one previously computed count and one low-bit addition.
spaceComplexity: O(1) auxiliary space excluding the O(n) output. The output array is the dynamic-programming table; loop indices need constant additional space.
attribution: Original repository-authored Blind75 C++ algorithm, promoted from the validated correct fixtures. Collection membership follows Crackr; no external solution service is used.
correctness: The bits of i consist of the bits of i shifted right once, followed by its low bit. Therefore popcount(i)=popcount(i>>1)+(i&1). The shifted value is smaller, so its count is already available while filling the table in increasing order.

edgeCases: The output includes every value from zero through n.

explanation: Repeat exactly 32 times: shift the result left, append the current low input bit, and shift the input right. Leading zeros are included.
timeComplexity: O(32), constant time for the fixed-width input. The loop executes exactly 32 fixed-cost rounds.
spaceComplexity: O(1) auxiliary space. Only the result, remaining input, and loop count are retained.
attribution: Original EPI Practice C# implementation, reusing and refining the repository-authored Blind75 algorithm fixtures. Collection membership follows Crackr; no external solution service is used.
correctness: After i rounds, result holds the reverse of the lowest i original bits. Shifting result and appending the next low bit preserves this invariant. Exactly 32 rounds include all leading zeros and produce the required unsigned 32-bit reversal.
walkthrough: For n=3, original bits 0 and 1 are set. Reversing 32 positions moves them to bits 31 and 30, giving 0xC0000000, or unsigned value 3221225472. Return that value in a long.
edgeCases: Exactly 32 bits are reversed, not all 64 bits of the carrier type.
The result is nonnegative in the range 0..2^32-1.
Leading zero bits are included.

correctness: The format includes all 32 bit positions, including leading zeros. Reversal maps original bit i to position 31-i; base-two parsing assigns exactly the numerical weight of each reversed position. Thus the returned nonnegative integer is the required fixed-width reversal.

explanation: XOR adds bits without carries. AND followed by a left shift produces the carry bits. Repeat until no carries remain, using the contract's signed 32-bit arithmetic.
timeComplexity: O(32), at most a constant number of carry-propagation rounds for 32-bit values. Every carry moves at least one position left, and fixed-width carries disappear after at most 32 rounds.
spaceComplexity: O(1) auxiliary space. Only the two current operands and carry pattern are retained.
attribution: Original EPI Practice C# implementation, reusing and refining the repository-authored Blind75 algorithm fixtures. Collection membership follows Crackr; no external solution service is used.
correctness: For fixed-width integers, a XOR b contains the sum bits without carries and (a AND b)<<1 contains exactly the pending carry bits. Replacing the operands with these values preserves their sum modulo 2^32. Carries move left until none remain, leaving the signed 32-bit sum.
walkthrough: For a=5 (0101) and b=3 (0011), XOR gives 0110=6 and shifted AND gives 0010=2. The next pair is (0100=4,0100=4), then (0000=0,1000=8), then (1000=8,0000=0). No carry remains, so return 8.
edgeCases: Negative operands use two’s-complement 32-bit arithmetic.
A zero operand needs no carry propagation.
The displayed input contract guarantees the mathematical sum fits a signed int.

explanation: Walk toward the largest key. If that node has a left subtree, its predecessor is the rightmost key in that subtree; otherwise its parent is the predecessor.
timeComplexity: O(h) time: the search follows a downward path to the maximum and at most another downward path in its left subtree, bounded by tree height h.
spaceComplexity: O(1) auxiliary space: only the current node and its parent are retained; no traversal stack is built.
attribution: Original EPI Practice implementation and explanation. Task identity and technical compatibility facts are attributed to Interview Cake; no course prose, examples, solution code or artwork are included. No affiliation is implied.
correctness: A node's predecessor is the largest key in its left subtree, if that subtree exists. Otherwise it is the closest ancestor for which the node lies in the ancestor's right subtree. For the globally largest node this ancestor is its parent, so these cases identify exactly the greatest key remaining after the maximum is excluded.
walkthrough: In the tree [12,5,20,2,9,17,25], the rightward search visits 12, 20 and 25. Node 25 has no left subtree, so its parent, 20, is the second-largest key. The tree remains unchanged.
edgeCases: Two nodes
largest node with a left branch
negative keys
skewed trees.
With two nodes, return the smaller key; if the maximum has a left subtree, use that subtree’s rightmost key rather than its parent.

explanation: Keep the lowest earlier price and the best profit seen. Evaluate a sale before allowing its own price to become the next minimum.
timeComplexity: O(n) time: each of the n-1 possible sale positions performs a constant number of comparisons.
spaceComplexity: O(1) auxiliary space: one earlier minimum and one best profit.
attribution: Original EPI Practice implementation and explanation. Task identity and technical compatibility facts are attributed to Interview Cake; no course prose, examples, solution code or artwork are included. No affiliation is implied.
correctness: Before each sale, the minimum contains precisely earlier prices. The best sale at that position uses that minimum; maximizing these candidates examines every legal pair implicitly.
walkthrough: For prices [11,7,13,4,10], the first feasible profit is 7-11=-4. Price 7 becomes the cheapest earlier purchase; selling at 13 improves the profit to 6. The later low price 4 followed by 10 also gives 6. Updating the minimum only after considering a sale prevents buying and selling at the same position.
edgeCases: Declining prices
equal prices
minimum at the final position.
For [19,14,8,3], return -5; initializing the best profit to zero would incorrectly allow skipping the mandatory trade.

explanation: Traverse nodes with their depths, tracking the smallest and largest depths encountered at leaves. Reject once their difference exceeds one.
timeComplexity: O(n) time: each of n nodes is pushed and visited at most once, with constant work per visit.
spaceComplexity: O(h) auxiliary space: depth-first pending siblings occupy at most a constant number of entries per tree level; h can be n.
attribution: Original EPI Practice implementation and explanation. Task identity and technical compatibility facts are attributed to Interview Cake; no course prose, examples, solution code or artwork are included. No affiliation is implied.
correctness: The stored extremes are exactly the extrema among visited leaves. The final spread is the required global condition; an excessive partial spread can never decrease when more leaves are visited.
walkthrough: For [4,2,7,1,3,null,9], the leaves are 1, 3 and 9. Each is two edges below the root, so the shallowest and deepest depths are both 2 and their difference is 0. Return true. A long chain would also return true because it has only one leaf.
edgeCases: Empty tree
one-leaf chain
leaf depths in separate subtrees. This is not per-node AVL height balance.
An empty tree returns true, and a chain of any supported length returns true because its only leaf supplies both depth extremes.

timeComplexity: O(n) time: each of n nodes is pushed and visited at most once, with constant work per visit.
spaceComplexity: O(h) auxiliary space: depth-first pending siblings occupy at most a constant number of entries per tree level; h can be n.
attribution: Original EPI Practice implementation and explanation. Task identity and technical compatibility facts are attributed to Interview Cake; no course prose, examples, solution code or artwork are included. No affiliation is implied.
correctness: The stored extremes are exactly the extrema among visited leaves. The final spread is the required global condition; an excessive partial spread can never decrease when more leaves are visited.
walkthrough: For [4,2,7,1,3,null,9], the leaves are 1, 3 and 9. Each is two edges below the root, so the shallowest and deepest depths are both 2 and their difference is 0. Return true. A long chain would also return true because it has only one leaf.

explanation: Use a depth-first stack of nodes and open lower/upper bounds inherited from ancestors. The initial sentinels lie outside all signed 32-bit keys. Tighten the upper bound for a left child and the lower bound for a right child.
timeComplexity: O(n) time: each node is checked once against two inherited bounds.
spaceComplexity: O(h) auxiliary space for pending branches or recursive frames along tree height h; O(n) on a skewed tree.
attribution: Original EPI Practice implementation and explanation. Task identity and technical compatibility facts are attributed to Interview Cake; no course prose, examples, solution code or artwork are included. No affiliation is implied.
correctness: Each bound summarizes every relevant ancestor restriction. Passing the current key as the new bound enforces all descendant restrictions inductively.
walkthrough: For [10,4,16,1,7,12,19], node 4 inherits an upper bound of 10; its right child 7 must lie strictly between 4 and 10. Node 16 inherits a lower bound of 10, and its left child 12 must lie between 10 and 16. Every inherited interval is respected, so the answer is true.

duplicates

explanation: Push openers onto a stack and compare each closer with the top. Reject a mismatch or an empty stack at a closer.
timeComplexity: O(n) time: inspect each character once, pushing and popping each delimiter at most once.
spaceComplexity: O(n) auxiliary space: an input consisting only of openers leaves n unmatched entries.
attribution: Original EPI Practice implementation and explanation. Task identity and technical compatibility facts are attributed to Interview Cake; no course prose, examples, solution code or artwork are included. No affiliation is implied.
correctness: The stack records exactly the unmatched openers in nesting order. A closer can legally match only the top, so each accepted match preserves the invariant.
walkthrough: Scanning a{b[c](d)}, ignore letters and push {, then [. The ] removes [, the ( is pushed and removed by ), and the final } removes {. No closer crosses another pair and the stack finishes empty, so return true.
edgeCases: Empty input
stray closer
unfinished opener
mixed delimiter kinds.
Empty or delimiter-free input returns true; ([)] returns false because ) cannot close the top [.

explanation: Maintain the next unread index in each source. Each served ID must consume the next ID from exactly one source.
timeComplexity: O(c+1) time for c served entries: each entry checks two current source heads; source arrays are not rescanned. With a valid interleaving c=a+b.
spaceComplexity: O(1) auxiliary space: two source indices, regardless of input lengths.
attribution: Original EPI Practice implementation and explanation. Task identity and technical compatibility facts are attributed to Interview Cake; no course prose, examples, solution code or artwork are included. No affiliation is implied.
correctness: At every step the consumed prefixes are exactly the source orders already served. Any different next ID violates at least one source order; exhausting both sources proves exact coverage.
walkthrough: For takeOut=[8,3], dineIn=[5,9], served=[5,8,3,9], consume 5 from the dine-in head, then 8 and 3 from takeout, then 9 from dine-in. Both source positions reach their ends exactly, so return true.
edgeCases: Either source empty
unknown or repeated served ID
missing orders.
Three empty arrays return true. A missing served order fails the final exhaustion check; an unknown or out-of-order ID fails when encountered.

explanation: Advance a pair holding consecutive Fibonacci numbers until the requested index is reached.
timeComplexity: O(n+1) time: a constant-size pair advances at most n times; n=0 takes constant work.
spaceComplexity: O(1) auxiliary space: only consecutive values and a loop counter are stored; the bounded bank domain uses fixed-width-size values.
attribution: Original EPI Practice implementation and explanation. Task identity and technical compatibility facts are attributed to Interview Cake; no course prose, examples, solution code or artwork are included. No affiliation is implied.
correctness: Before each iteration i<n, previous is F(i) and current is F(i+1). Assigning previous=current produces the next required result; the sum prepares the next iteration. At n=46 the final unused current overflows signed 32-bit arithmetic, but previous already holds the exact F(46), which is returned. No subsequent computation uses that overflowed value.
walkthrough: For n=6, start with F(0)=0 and F(1)=1. Advancing the two running values produces 1, 2, 3, 5 and 8 for indices 2 through 6. The required result is 8; there is no recursive tree of repeated work.
edgeCases: Indices zero and one
largest supported index.
F(0)=0 and F(1)=1; the maximum supported result is F(46)=1836311903.

explanation: Copy the successor's payload into the target and link the target directly to the successor's successor.
timeComplexity: O(1) time: read the successor and replace exactly the target’s Value and Next fields.
spaceComplexity: O(1) auxiliary space: retain at most one successor reference; allocate no list nodes.
attribution: Original EPI Practice implementation and explanation. Task identity and technical compatibility facts are attributed to Interview Cake; no course prose, examples, solution code or artwork are included. No affiliation is implied.
correctness: Every path before the target is unchanged. Replacing the target value and bypassing its successor removes exactly the target position from the value sequence while preserving the required target identity.
walkthrough: The list is 9 -> 4 -> 7 -> 2 and the supplied target is the node currently holding 4. Copy 7 into that same target object and point it to the node holding 2. The head-to-tail values become [9,7,2]. An alias to the target now observes 7, while an alias to the bypassed successor still refers to its separate, unchanged object. The callable receives only the target node and returns void/None/undefined. JSON supplies [listValues,targetIndex]; expected is the reachable value sequence after mutation, with identity checked separately.
edgeCases: Target is head
target immediately precedes tail
repeated values
aliases to bypassed successor.
Deleting the head of [3,6] leaves that same head object holding 6 with Next=null. A tail target is outside the valid bank domain.

walkthrough: The list is 9 -> 4 -> 7 -> 2 and the supplied target is the node currently holding 4. Copy 7 into that same target object and point it to the node holding 2. The head-to-tail values become [9,7,2]. An alias to the target now observes 7, while an alias to the bypassed successor still refers to its separate, unchanged object. The callable receives only the target node and returns void/None/undefined. JSON supplies [listValues,targetIndex]; expected is the reachable value sequence after mutation, with identity checked separately.
edgeCases: Target is head
target immediately precedes tail
repeated values
aliases to bypassed successor.
Deleting the head of [3,6] leaves that same head object holding 6 with Next=null. A tail target is outside the valid bank domain.

explanation: Move one pointer by one link and another by two. They meet exactly when a reachable cycle exists.
timeComplexity: O(n) time: an acyclic fast pointer reaches null after at most n links; after entering a cycle, the relative offset advances by one and meets within at most n more steps.
spaceComplexity: O(1) auxiliary space: two node references, with no visited set.
attribution: Original EPI Practice implementation and explanation. Task identity and technical compatibility facts are attributed to Interview Cake; no course prose, examples, solution code or artwork are included. No affiliation is implied.
correctness: Without a cycle the faster pointer reaches null. Within a cycle its relative position advances by one per iteration and eventually equals the slower pointer.
walkthrough: For values [2,2,9] with tail link -1, the last node points to null. The repeated payload 2 does not imply a cycle: the two nodes are different objects. The fast pointer reaches the end, so return false. JSON supplies [listValues,tailLinkIndex]; -1 means a null tail. The callable receives only the constructed entry node and returns a boolean based on node identity.
edgeCases: Empty entry
self-loop
equal values without a cycle
noncyclic prefix.
An empty entry returns false. A node pointing to itself returns true; distinct nodes with equal values do not constitute a cycle.

explanation: Group files by size and a fingerprint of at most 64 bytes each at the beginning, middle and end. For each matching pair, orient the paths by modification time.
timeComplexity: Expected O(f+d) filesystem visits for f files and d directories, plus total path-character handling; each file reads at most 3*64 bytes and makes a constant number of metadata/seek operations. Hash grouping is expected constant time per bounded fingerprint.
spaceComplexity: O(f) bounded fingerprints plus stored path characters and directory traversal state; returned pairs add path storage. The bound is independent of total file-content bytes.
attribution: Original EPI Practice implementation and explanation. Task identity and technical compatibility facts are attributed to Interview Cake; no course prose, examples, solution code or artwork are included. No affiliation is implied.
correctness: Equal fingerprints identify exactly the candidate groups defined by the adapter. Traversing every directory visits each file, and grouping retains enough information to emit each pair once without a full-content scan.
walkthrough: The controlled directory contains a.txt and nested/b.txt, both with the bytes "same bytes". Their sizes and all three bounded samples match. Their modification times are 1000 and 2000, so report their full paths with a.txt first as the earlier-time candidate. This orientation is a heuristic, and equal fingerprints can still be false positives; neither file is changed. JSON supplies controlled file descriptors. The callable receives the temporary directory’s full path and returns FilePaths pairs containing full paths; displayed expected paths are relative to that directory.
edgeCases: Empty directory
nested and sibling directories
zero-byte files
equal timestamps
deliberate sample collisions. No file deletion or writes.
Empty directories return no pairs. Two empty files have identical fingerprints; equal timestamps permit either orientation. Matching sampled bytes do not prove equal complete content.

explanation: Bisect the value range. Count values in the lower half; if its population exceeds its capacity, a duplicate lies there, otherwise one lies in the upper half.
timeComplexity: O(n log n) time: halving the n-value search interval takes O(log n) rounds, each scanning all n+1 entries.
spaceComplexity: O(1) auxiliary space: interval endpoints, midpoint and count only; input is read-only.
attribution: Original EPI Practice implementation and explanation. Task identity and technical compatibility facts are attributed to Interview Cake; no course prose, examples, solution code or artwork are included. No affiliation is implied.
correctness: The maintained interval contains more array occurrences than distinct possible values after discarding the other half when safe. Pigeonhole counting therefore keeps a duplicate until a single value remains.
walkthrough: For [1,3,4,2,3], candidate values are 1..4. The lower half 1..2 contains two entries, fitting its two slots, so continue in 3..4. Value 3 alone appears twice but has only one available slot; narrowing finishes at 3. Every pass reads the same unchanged input.
edgeCases: Several repeated values
one value repeated many times
smallest valid array.
[1,1] returns 1 without a counting pass. Multiple repeated values are allowed; any actual duplicate passes.

explanation: Bisect candidate values using the count C(m) of all entries at most midpoint m, comparing that count with the m available values in 1..m. Keep the half whose endpoint counts still bracket excess population.
timeComplexity: O(n log n) time: halving the n-value search interval takes O(log n) rounds, each scanning all n+1 entries.
spaceComplexity: O(1) auxiliary space: interval endpoints, midpoint and count only; input is read-only.
attribution: Original EPI Practice implementation and explanation. Task identity and technical compatibility facts are attributed to Interview Cake; no course prose, examples, solution code or artwork are included. No affiliation is implied.
correctness: Maintain C(lower-1)<=lower-1 and C(upper)>upper. Initially C(0)=0 and C(n)=n+1. If C(mid)>mid, set upper=mid; otherwise set lower=mid+1. At the final value v, C(v)>v and C(v-1)<=v-1, so their difference, the number of v entries, is at least two. This argument does not assume that C(m)>m is monotone.
walkthrough: For [1,3,4,2,3], lower=1 and upper=4. At midpoint 2, C(2)=2, so lower becomes 3. At midpoint 3, C(3)=4>3, so upper becomes 3. Return 3. Counts cover the whole prefix 1..midpoint, not just the current interval; the endpoint invariant guarantees that the final value repeats.
edgeCases: Several repeated values
one value repeated many times
smallest valid array.
[1,1] returns 1 without a counting pass. Multiple repeated values are allowed; any actual duplicate passes.

explanation: Interpret index-to-value links as a functional graph. Use a slow/fast meeting followed by equal-speed pointers to locate a cycle entry that is a repeated value.
timeComplexity: O(n) time: Floyd’s meeting phase traverses a prefix and cycle of at most n+1 indices; the entry phase takes at most the prefix length.
spaceComplexity: O(1) auxiliary space: a fixed number of index walkers, with no copied array or visited set.
attribution: Original EPI Practice implementation and explanation. Task identity and technical compatibility facts are attributed to Interview Cake; no course prose, examples, solution code or artwork are included. No affiliation is implied.
correctness: Starting at the extra index creates a path into a cycle. The entry has an incoming edge from both its cycle predecessor and the entering path, so its value appears at least twice. Floyd's second phase identifies that entry.
walkthrough: Treat index i as pointing to numbers[i]. In [4,1,3,4,2], the path from index 0 is 0 -> 4 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4, with cycle entry 4. Slow and fast pointers meet in that cycle; moving one pointer back to 0 and advancing both identifies entry 4, a repeated array value.
edgeCases: Cycle near the start
several valid duplicate answers
values repeated more than twice.
[1,1] returns 1; other valid inputs may contain several duplicate values, so no particular duplicate is mandated.

explanation: View each array entry as the next-index pointer. Run Floyd’s slow/fast search starting at numbers[0], then reset slow to that same start and advance both one step to the cycle entry.
timeComplexity: O(n) time: Floyd’s meeting phase traverses a prefix and cycle of at most n+1 indices; the entry phase takes at most the prefix length.
spaceComplexity: O(1) auxiliary space: a fixed number of index walkers, with no copied array or visited set.
attribution: Original EPI Practice implementation and explanation. Task identity and technical compatibility facts are attributed to Interview Cake; no course prose, examples, solution code or artwork are included. No affiliation is implied.
correctness: The path from index 0 enters a cycle because all links are in 1..n, excluding 0. Its entry has two distinct incoming source indices: the path predecessor and the cycle predecessor. Starting Floyd at numbers[0] removes the first path edge but preserves this entry (or starts directly on it). At a meeting, the faster walker has gained whole cycle lengths; resetting one walker to the chosen start makes equal-speed walkers meet at the entry.
walkthrough: For [4,1,3,4,2], start both walkers at numbers[0]=4. After successive moves (slow,fast) is (2,3), (3,2), then (4,4). Reset slow to 4; the walkers already agree, so return 4. In the full path 0 -> 4 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4, indices 0 and 3 both point to 4, proving it is repeated.
edgeCases: Cycle near the start
several valid duplicate answers
values repeated more than twice.
[1,1] returns 1; other valid inputs may contain several duplicate values, so no particular duplicate is mandated.

explanation: Compare the middle word with the right boundary. The smallest word remains in the half containing the ordering break, or at the middle boundary.
timeComplexity: O(log n) comparisons because each step halves the candidate interval; comparing words may inspect L characters, giving O(L log n) character work.
spaceComplexity: O(1) auxiliary space: only three indices and references to existing words.
attribution: Original EPI Practice implementation and explanation. Task identity and technical compatibility facts are attributed to Interview Cake; no course prose, examples, solution code or artwork are included. No affiliation is implied.
correctness: If the middle word is greater than the right word, a wrap occurs after the middle. Otherwise the minimum cannot lie strictly after the middle. Shrinking these bounds leaves its exact index.
walkthrough: For [mint,oak,ant,birch,cedar], middle index 2 contains ant, which is less than cedar at upper index 4, so set upper=2. Next middle index 1 contains oak, greater than ant, so set lower=2. The bounds meet at index 2, the minimum ant; return 2 without changing the array.
edgeCases: Singleton
rotation by one
unrotated input under the stated bank extension.
A singleton or unrotated sorted array returns index 0 under the bank convention; duplicate words and empty arrays are excluded.
