explanation: For each node, collect colors already used by its neighbors and choose a palette color outside that set.
timeComplexity: Expected O(V+E) time: neighbor scans total 2E in an undirected graph, and the first degree(v)+1 distinct palette entries must include an available color. Hash membership is expected O(1), treating color names as bounded-size keys.
spaceComplexity: O(D+1) auxiliary space: the current node’s forbidden-color set contains at most D neighbor colors, and is discarded before the next node.
attribution: Original EPI Practice implementation and explanation. Task identity and technical compatibility facts are attributed to Interview Cake; no course prose, examples, solution code or artwork are included. No affiliation is implied.
correctness: At most degree(node) colors are forbidden by its neighbors. A prefix of degree(node)+1 distinct colors therefore contains an available color. A later neighbor avoids this assigned color, so every edge remains valid.
walkthrough: For the triangle with adjacency [[1,2],[0,2],[0,1]] and palette [red,blue,green], assign red to v0, blue to v1 because v0 is red, and green to v2 because its neighbors use both red and blue. Every edge has different endpoint colors. Any other valid assignment also passes; the displayed true reports successful properties. JSON supplies [adjacency,palette]; the callable receives graph nodes and colors and returns void/None/undefined. Expected true is the checker verdict for legal Color mutations and preserved graph identity/links.
edgeCases: Disconnected components
isolated nodes
complete graph
empty graph.
An empty graph needs no assignments. Isolated nodes can all use the first color. A clique of D+1 nodes uses D+1 distinct colors.

explanation: Track the largest and smallest one-value and two-value products while scanning. Each new value can extend either extreme two-value product to a three-value candidate.
timeComplexity: O(n) time: one pass maintains a fixed set of extrema with constant work per value.
spaceComplexity: O(1) auxiliary space: the extrema and candidate product are scalars; the input is never sorted or copied.
attribution: Original EPI Practice implementation and explanation. Task identity and technical compatibility facts are attributed to Interview Cake; no course prose, examples, solution code or artwork are included. No affiliation is implied.
correctness: Multiplication by a new negative value reverses order, so both extremes are sufficient. Updating three-value candidates before pairs and pairs before singles guarantees distinct positions.
walkthrough: For [-8,-5,2,4], the first two negatives have product 40. Combining that pair with 2 gives 80, and later with 4 gives 160. Selecting the three numerically largest values would miss this result; tracking both low and high pair products preserves the winning candidate.
edgeCases: All negative
two large-magnitude negatives
zeros
repeated extrema.
For [-6,-3,-2,-1], return -6, even though it is negative. Equal values at different positions remain distinct eligible factors.

explanation: Keep the three largest entries and the two smallest entries during one pass. Compare the product of the largest three with the product of the largest entry and the two smallest entries.
timeComplexity: O(n) time: one pass maintains a fixed set of extrema with constant work per value.
spaceComplexity: O(1) auxiliary space: the extrema and candidate product are scalars; the input is never sorted or copied.
attribution: Original EPI Practice implementation and explanation. Task identity and technical compatibility facts are attributed to Interview Cake; no course prose, examples, solution code or artwork are included. No affiliation is implied.
correctness: The extrema track occurrences, not distinct values, so equal entries can fill multiple slots. With a positive factor, the best remaining pair is either the two largest positives or the two most negative values. If every value is nonpositive, the three largest values give the least-negative product (or zero). Thus one of the two candidate products is optimal, including all-negative and zero cases.
walkthrough: For [-8,-5,2,4], the final three largest entries are 4,2,-5 and the two smallest are -8,-5. The candidate products are 4*2*(-5)=-40 and 4*(-8)*(-5)=160. Return 160; keeping only the three largest entries would lose the winning negative pair.

explanation: Push new items to an input stack. When the output stack is empty, transfer all input items into it; this reverses their order once.
timeComplexity: O(1) amortized per operation: each item is pushed to incoming, transferred once, then popped from outgoing. A single transfer-triggering Dequeue can cost O(q); m operations cost O(m).
spaceComplexity: O(q) persistent space: each of q queued occurrences lives in exactly one of the two stacks.
attribution: Original EPI Practice implementation and explanation. Task identity and technical compatibility facts are attributed to Interview Cake; no course prose, examples, solution code or artwork are included. No affiliation is implied.
correctness: The output stack top is always the oldest remaining item. Transfer is performed only when it is empty, so newer items never pass older ones. Each item is moved at most once.
walkthrough: Enqueue 4 and 9 into the incoming stack. The first Dequeue moves them to the outgoing stack and removes 4. Enqueue 2 without moving the still-pending 9. The next Dequeue removes 9; only then does transferring the incoming stack expose 2. The returned values are 4, 9 and 2 in FIFO order. JSON supplies [operationNames,argumentLists] for one fresh QueueTwoStacks. Void operations display null; Dequeue displays the returned item or {"error":"empty"}.
edgeCases: Empty and drained queue
alternating operations
duplicate values.
Dequeue on a fresh or drained queue throws an empty-state exception, normalized to {"error":"empty"}; duplicate values remain separate occurrences.

explanation: For each position i, choose uniformly among positions i through n-1 and exchange the chosen value into position i.
timeComplexity: O(n) time: a constant-time random choice and swap fixes one position per iteration.
spaceComplexity: O(1) auxiliary space: only indices and a swap temporary; all rearrangement uses the original array.
attribution: Original EPI Practice implementation and explanation. Task identity and technical compatibility facts are attributed to Interview Cake; no course prose, examples, solution code or artwork are included. No affiliation is implied.
correctness: At position i each remaining occurrence has probability 1/(n-i) of being selected. Multiplying conditional probabilities gives 1/n! for each full occurrence permutation.
walkthrough: Starting with [4,8,1], position 0 chooses uniformly among all three occurrences. If it selects index 2, the array becomes [1,8,4]. Position 1 then chooses index 1 or 2 equally, producing [1,8,4] or [1,4,8]. Each full three-element permutation has probability 1/(3*2)=1/6. The judge returns true when these distribution and in-place properties hold. The callable mutates the supplied array and returns void/None/undefined. Expected true is the checker verdict for occurrence preservation, identity, legal source use and unbiased permutations; it is not a particular array result.
edgeCases: Empty/singleton arrays
duplicate values
possibility of retaining original positions.
Empty and singleton arrays remain unchanged. Repeated values are separate occurrences; unbiased occurrence permutations may have the same visible value sequence.

explanation: Work from the last position toward index 1. At position i, choose uniformly from the still-unfixed prefix 0..i, using inclusive bounds, and swap that occurrence into i.
timeComplexity: O(n) time: a constant-time random choice and swap fixes one position per iteration.
spaceComplexity: O(1) auxiliary space: only indices and a swap temporary; all rearrangement uses the original array.
attribution: Original EPI Practice implementation and explanation. Task identity and technical compatibility facts are attributed to Interview Cake; no course prose, examples, solution code or artwork are included. No affiliation is implied.
correctness: Before fixing i, the suffix after i is final and all other occurrences remain in 0..i. Each has conditional probability 1/(i+1) of being chosen. Multiplying n,n-1,...,2 choice probabilities gives 1/n! for every occurrence permutation.
walkthrough: For [4,8,1], start at i=2 and draw from 0..2. If chosen=0, swap to [1,8,4], fixing 4 at the end. At i=1, choose 0 or 1, producing [8,1,4] or [1,8,4]. Each full permutation has probability 1/(3*2)=1/6. The method returns no array; true is the adapter’s distribution and mutation verdict. The callable mutates the supplied array and returns void/None/undefined. Expected true is the checker verdict for occurrence preservation, identity, legal source use and unbiased permutations; it is not a particular array result.

explanation: Before inserting a duration into a set, check whether its complement has appeared earlier.
timeComplexity: Expected O(n) time: each duration performs one hash lookup and at most one insertion.
spaceComplexity: O(n) auxiliary space: the set may retain every distinct earlier duration.

explanation: Move a leading pointer k steps, then advance a second pointer with it until the leading pointer reaches null.
timeComplexity: O(n) time: lead advances n times in total and follow at most n-k times.
spaceComplexity: O(1) auxiliary space: two references and an offset counter; no nodes are copied.
attribution: Original EPI Practice implementation and explanation. Task identity and technical compatibility facts are attributed to Interview Cake; no course prose, examples, solution code or artwork are included. No affiliation is implied.
correctness: The pointers stay k links apart. When the leading pointer is past the tail, the second pointer is exactly k positions from the end.
walkthrough: For k=2 and list 5 -> 8 -> 1 -> 6, advance the leading pointer two nodes to 1. Move both pointers together until the leading pointer passes the tail; the following pointer then refers to the original node holding 1. Its zero-based identity index is 2, which is the adapter output; the method returns that node object. JSON supplies [k,listValues]. The callable returns the original node object; the adapter displays its zero-based index in the original list, not its value and not k.
edgeCases: Select head
select tail
repeated payloads must not confuse identity.
k=1 returns the original tail object; k=n returns the original head. Values are irrelevant to identity, and invalid k is outside the bank domain.

explanation: Maintain the item stack and a second stack of running maxima, retaining repeated maximum occurrences.
timeComplexity: O(1) per operation under the stack push/pop cost model (amortized for dynamically grown arrays): only a constant number of stack operations occur.
spaceComplexity: O(s) persistent space for s live entries, including their stored maximum information.
attribution: Original EPI Practice implementation and explanation. Task identity and technical compatibility facts are attributed to Interview Cake; no course prose, examples, solution code or artwork are included. No affiliation is implied.
correctness: Each stored maximum equals the maximum of the matching stack prefix. Push extends that invariant and Pop restores the preceding prefix; GetMax simply reads it.
walkthrough: Push 5, then 9. The auxiliary maximum stack records both increases, so GetMax returns 9. Pop removes 9 from both stacks. The remaining maximum is 5, and the next GetMax reads it without removing it. Equal maxima would each need a retained occurrence as well. JSON supplies [operationNames,argumentLists] for one fresh MaxStack. Push displays null; Pop/GetMax display integer results or {"error":"empty"}.
edgeCases: Negative values
repeated maxima
empty/drained state
repeated GetMax calls.
After pushing 8 twice and popping once, GetMax still returns 8. Empty Pop/GetMax raise an exception normalized to {"error":"empty"}.

explanation: Store a pair (item,maximum-so-far) at every stack depth. Push computes the new maximum from the item and the previous top’s cached maximum; Pop removes one pair and GetMax reads the top pair’s second field.
timeComplexity: O(1) per operation under the stack push/pop cost model (amortized for dynamically grown arrays): only a constant number of stack operations occur.
spaceComplexity: O(s) persistent space for s live entries, including their stored maximum information.
attribution: Original EPI Practice implementation and explanation. Task identity and technical compatibility facts are attributed to Interview Cake; no course prose, examples, solution code or artwork are included. No affiliation is implied.
correctness: By induction, each entry’s second field is the maximum of all items at or below that depth. Push extends this prefix maximum, and Pop reveals the already-correct maximum for the remaining prefix. Equal maxima need no special removal rule because every depth has its own snapshot.
walkthrough: Push 5 to store (5,5), then push 9 to store (9,9). GetMax reads 9 from the top pair. Pop returns its item 9 and removes that pair; GetMax now reads 5 from (5,5). Two pushes of 8 create two (8,8) entries, so one pop still leaves maximum 8. JSON supplies [operationNames,argumentLists] for one fresh MaxStack. Push displays null; Pop/GetMax display integer results or {"error":"empty"}.
edgeCases: Negative values
repeated maxima
empty/drained state
repeated GetMax calls.
After pushing 8 twice and popping once, GetMax still returns 8. Empty Pop/GetMax raise an exception normalized to {"error":"empty"}.

explanation: Maintain parallel value and prefix-maximum stacks of equal depth. Every Push stores both the item and max(item,previous maximum), even when the maximum is unchanged. Pop removes one entry from each; GetMax peeks at the maximum stack.
timeComplexity: O(1) per operation under the stack push/pop cost model (amortized for dynamically grown arrays): only a constant number of stack operations occur.
spaceComplexity: O(s) persistent space for s live entries, including their stored maximum information.
attribution: Original EPI Practice implementation and explanation. Task identity and technical compatibility facts are attributed to Interview Cake; no course prose, examples, solution code or artwork are included. No affiliation is implied.
correctness: At each depth the maximum stack stores the maximum of the matching value prefix. Pushing extends that invariant; removing the top entries restores the invariant for the shorter prefix. Repeated maxima persist in separate snapshots, so popping one occurrence cannot erase the remaining maximum.
walkthrough: Push 5: values=[5], maxima=[5]. Push 9: values=[5,9], maxima=[5,9]. GetMax returns 9. Pop removes one entry from both stacks and returns 9; GetMax now returns 5. If the second push had been 4, maxima would instead be [5,5], because every depth gets a snapshot. JSON supplies [operationNames,argumentLists] for one fresh MaxStack. Push displays null; Pop/GetMax display integer results or {"error":"empty"}.
edgeCases: Negative values
repeated maxima
empty/drained state
repeated GetMax calls.
After pushing 8 twice and popping once, GetMax still returns 8. Empty Pop/GetMax raise an exception normalized to {"error":"empty"}.

explanation: Set ways[0]=1. Process denominations one at a time, adding ways[a-coin] into ways[a] for increasing amounts.
timeComplexity: O(A*d+A+d+1) time for amount A and d denominations: initialize A+1 cells, then visit up to A cells per denomination. This also covers empty denominations and amount zero.
spaceComplexity: O(A+1) auxiliary space: one count per subtotal from 0 through A.
attribution: Original EPI Practice implementation and explanation. Task identity and technical compatibility facts are attributed to Interview Cake; no course prose, examples, solution code or artwork are included. No affiliation is implied.
correctness: After processing a denomination prefix, ways[a] counts exactly combinations using that prefix. Increasing amounts permits repeated use of the current coin; processing each coin once avoids counting orderings.
walkthrough: For amount 8 and denominations [2,3,5], the three unordered combinations are 2+2+2+2, 2+3+3, and 3+5. Processing each denomination in the outer loop adds each combination once; 5+3 is the same combination as 3+5, not a fourth answer.
edgeCases: Zero target
no denominations
unreachable target
coins larger than target.
Amount zero has one combination (choose no coins), even with no denominations. Positive amount with no usable coins has zero combinations.

explanation: Read the smallest unconsumed head from either input until both are exhausted.
timeComplexity: O(a+b) time: each of the a+b input occurrences is appended exactly once.
spaceComplexity: O(a+b) result storage and O(1) auxiliary space beyond the new result and two source indices.
attribution: Original EPI Practice implementation and explanation. Task identity and technical compatibility facts are attributed to Interview Cake; no course prose, examples, solution code or artwork are included. No affiliation is implied.
correctness: The smallest remaining item must be at one of the two heads. Appending that head preserves the sorted prefix and consumes every occurrence exactly once.
walkthrough: Merge [1,4,4] and [2,4,9] by repeatedly taking the smaller head: 1, then 2, then the three occurrences of 4, then 9. The new output is [1,2,4,4,4,9]; neither input is sorted again or modified.
edgeCases: Empty inputs
repeated keys
one input entirely precedes the other.
Empty inputs produce a new empty result; if only one input is empty, copy the other. Equal values are retained with their full multiplicity.

explanation: Sort copies by start, then extend the current output interval while the next interval begins no later than its end.
timeComplexity: O(n log n+n) time: sort n meeting references by start, then process each once.
spaceComplexity: O(n) auxiliary space for the sorted reference copy and up to n newly allocated result intervals; original intervals are untouched.
attribution: Original EPI Practice implementation and explanation. Task identity and technical compatibility facts are attributed to Interview Cake; no course prose, examples, solution code or artwork are included. No affiliation is implied.
correctness: Once intervals are sorted, a gap before the next start means no later interval can bridge it. Otherwise joining the ranges preserves exactly their union.
walkthrough: Sort [[9,12],[1,4],[4,7],[10,14]] by start to obtain [1,4], [4,7], [9,12], [10,14]. The first two touch and become [1,7]. The last two overlap and become [9,14]. The gap from 7 to 9 remains, giving [[1,7],[9,14]] in newly allocated meeting objects. JSON intervals are [StartTime,EndTime] pairs; return newly allocated Meeting objects in increasing start order and preserve the supplied list and objects.
edgeCases: Touching boundaries
containment
duplicate intervals
a chain of overlaps
empty extension.
Touching [1,4] and [4,7] merge to [1,7]. An interval contained in another adds no extent; empty input returns an empty new list.

explanation: Breadth-first search records the predecessor of each first-discovered vertex. Reconstruct the route backward from the destination.
timeComplexity: Expected O(V+E) time: each discovered vertex is enqueued once and each outgoing adjacency entry examined at most once; reconstruction visits at most V predecessors. Labels are treated as bounded-size hash keys.
spaceComplexity: O(V) auxiliary space for the queue and predecessor map, plus an O(V) result route.
attribution: Original EPI Practice implementation and explanation. Task identity and technical compatibility facts are attributed to Interview Cake; no course prose, examples, solution code or artwork are included. No affiliation is implied.
correctness: BFS discovers vertices in nondecreasing distance from start. A predecessor chain from first discovery therefore has minimum edge count; the visited set prevents cycling.
walkthrough: In the network a:{b,c}, b:{a,d}, c:{a,d}, d:{b,c}, breadth-first search visits b and c at distance 1 and discovers d at distance 2. Reconstructing via b gives [a,b,d]. The equally short route [a,c,d] is also valid; both contain two edges. JSON supplies an adjacency map and two endpoint labels. Return any shortest route including endpoints; the adapter accepts tied routes and a no-route result.
edgeCases: Tied shortest routes
source equals destination
disconnected graph
cycles.
start=end returns [start]. A disconnected destination returns no route; tied shortest paths may use different valid predecessor choices.

explanation: Store a trie edge per next character and an explicit terminal flag at complete keys.
timeComplexity: Expected O(L+1) time per insertion: follow or create one hash-map edge per character of a length-L key, then inspect its terminal marker.
spaceComplexity: O(P+1) persistent trie storage for P distinct nonempty prefixes; each new key creates only its missing prefixes.
attribution: Original EPI Practice implementation and explanation. Task identity and technical compatibility facts are attributed to Interview Cake; no course prose, examples, solution code or artwork are included. No affiliation is implied.
correctness: The path represents a key's exact characters. Only its terminal flag denotes complete-key membership, so shared prefixes never create false complete keys.
walkthrough: Insert https://a/b: create missing character links and mark its final node, returning true. Insert https://a next: its character path exists, but its final node was not a complete key, so return true. Repeating https://a/b returns false. Extending it to https://a/b/c marks a different complete key and returns true. JSON supplies [operationNames,argumentLists] for one fresh Trie. Each AddWord receives one exact string and returns whether that complete key was newly inserted.
edgeCases: Duplicate keys
empty key
shorter prefix inserted after longer key
case-sensitive keys.
The empty key marks the root and returns true once, then false. Inserting a shorter prefix after a longer key returns true if its terminal marker was unset.

explanation: Scan starting at the designated opening parenthesis, including it in the depth count. Increment for each opener and decrement for each closer; the first decrement to zero identifies its matching closer.
timeComplexity: O(n) worst-case time: scan forward from the supplied opener until its match, visiting each intervening character once.
spaceComplexity: O(1) auxiliary space: an integer depth replaces a stack because only one bracket type matters.
attribution: Original EPI Practice implementation and explanation. Task identity and technical compatibility facts are attributed to Interview Cake; no course prose, examples, solution code or artwork are included. No affiliation is implied.
correctness: The depth tracks unmatched parentheses from the designated opener. A closer belongs to that opener exactly when all nested pairs have closed; the scan returns that position before considering later unrelated pairs.
walkthrough: In x(ab(cd)e)y, the opener at index 1 starts depth 1. The opener at index 4 increases depth to 2, its closer at index 7 reduces it to 1, and the closer at index 9 reduces it to 0. Return index 9 rather than the first closing parenthesis.
edgeCases: Immediately adjacent pair
deeply nested pairs
irrelevant characters
later unrelated pairs.
An adjacent () returns the next index; nested pairs must close before the designated pair. The bank guarantees that a matching closer exists.

explanation: Toggle each letter in a set of odd-frequency letters. A palindrome permits at most one odd frequency.
timeComplexity: O(n) time: each of n letters toggles one parity and the final odd count is checked.
spaceComplexity: O(1) auxiliary space for the fixed 26-letter domain, except a language implementation that copies the input characters as noted below.
attribution: Original EPI Practice implementation and explanation. Task identity and technical compatibility facts are attributed to Interview Cake; no course prose, examples, solution code or artwork are included. No affiliation is implied.
correctness: Mirrored positions use characters in pairs, leaving at most one center occurrence. Conversely, pairing each even part and placing the possible odd remainder at the center constructs a palindrome.
walkthrough: For aabbc, toggling odd-frequency membership removes a after its second occurrence and removes b after its second. Only c remains odd. It can occupy the middle of a palindrome such as abcba, so return true without enumerating reorderings.
edgeCases: Empty input
single letter
many repeated letters
two odd counts.
The empty string is a palindrome permutation. aabc returns false because both b and c have odd counts.

explanation: Write left-prefix products into the output, then multiply them by a running right-suffix product while scanning backward.
timeComplexity: O(n) time: two passes each perform a constant number of multiplications per position.
spaceComplexity: O(n) result storage and O(1) additional auxiliary space: only running prefix/suffix products and indices.
attribution: Original EPI Practice implementation and explanation. Task identity and technical compatibility facts are attributed to Interview Cake; no course prose, examples, solution code or artwork are included. No affiliation is implied.
correctness: Before the reverse scan, output[i] contains precisely factors left of i. The suffix contains precisely factors right of i, so multiplying them excludes exactly the required position.
walkthrough: For [2,0,-3,4], the left-product pass writes [1,2,0,0]. Multiplying right products into those entries gives [0,-24,0,0]. At the zero position, the other values multiply to 2*(-3)*4=-24; every other position includes the zero. Division is unnecessary.
edgeCases: One zero
several zeros
negatives
two entries.
One zero leaves only its own result potentially nonzero; two zeros make every result zero. No division or special zero branch is needed.

explanation: Intersect the x intervals and y intervals separately. Both resulting lengths must be positive.
timeComplexity: O(1) time: four endpoint comparisons and at most two subtractions determine the intersection.
spaceComplexity: O(1) auxiliary and result space: a fixed number of coordinates and one new Rectangle.
attribution: Original EPI Practice implementation and explanation. Task identity and technical compatibility facts are attributed to Interview Cake; no course prose, examples, solution code or artwork are included. No affiliation is implied.
correctness: A coordinate belongs to the overlap exactly when it lies in both corresponding intervals. Their common lower endpoint is the maximum lower endpoint and their upper endpoint is the minimum upper endpoint.
walkthrough: Rectangle [1,2,6,4] spans x=1..7 and y=2..6; [4,0,5,4] spans x=4..9 and y=0..4. The common x interval is 4..7 and the common y interval is 2..4, so return a new rectangle [4,2,3,2]. Both dimensions are positive. JSON rectangles are [LeftX,BottomY,Width,Height]; return a new Rectangle, including [0,0,0,0] when overlap has no positive area.
edgeCases: Containment
identical rectangles
edge or corner contact
negative coordinates.
Edge or corner contact returns a new [0,0,0,0] rectangle because at least one overlap dimension is zero. Containment returns the smaller rectangle’s geometry in a fresh object.

explanation: Recursively permute the suffix, then insert the removed first character at every position of each smaller permutation. A set removes duplicate strings.
timeComplexity: Expected O(n*n!) worst-case time: with distinct characters there are n! output strings, each constructed/hashed in O(n); all smaller recursion levels are dominated by this bound.
spaceComplexity: O(n*n!) worst-case result and intermediate string storage, plus recursion depth O(n); repeated characters can reduce the number of distinct results.
attribution: Original EPI Practice implementation and explanation. Task identity and technical compatibility facts are attributed to Interview Cake; no course prose, examples, solution code or artwork are included. No affiliation is implied.
correctness: Every permutation has some position occupied by the removed character; deleting it yields a suffix permutation generated recursively. Reinserting at all positions therefore covers every result, and the set prevents duplicates.
walkthrough: For ab, recurse on b to obtain the set {b}. Insert a before b and after b, yielding {ab,ba}. The base case for an empty suffix is the singleton set containing the empty string, which makes the first insertion possible. Return a set of strings; the adapter displays a JSON array and compares membership without imposing output order.
edgeCases: Empty string has one permutation
singleton
repeated characters under the bank extension.
Empty input returns the singleton set {""}; repeated characters yield distinct strings only, not repeated output entries.

explanation: Count each distinct character, then recursively extend a prefix with any character whose remaining count is positive. Decrement before recursion and restore after it so sibling choices see the original counts.
timeComplexity: Expected O(n*n!) worst-case time: with distinct characters there are n! output strings, each constructed/hashed in O(n); all smaller recursion levels are dominated by this bound.
spaceComplexity: O(n*n!) worst-case output storage. Outside the output, the count map and recursion depth are O(n); immutable prefixes retained along a recursion path can total O(n²) characters.
attribution: Original EPI Practice implementation and explanation. Task identity and technical compatibility facts are attributed to Interview Cake; no course prose, examples, solution code or artwork are included. No affiliation is implied.
correctness: Each recursive state has used exactly the prefix multiset and retains exactly the unused occurrences. Choosing a positive-count character preserves this invariant; reaching full length uses every occurrence. Every distinct target string determines one available next-character choice at each level, so all and only distinct permutations are reached.
walkthrough: For ab, counts start as {a:1,b:1}. Choose a, leaving only b and emitting ab; restore the counts. Choose b, leaving only a and emitting ba. For aa, there is only one available character choice at either level, so aa is emitted once. Empty input immediately emits the empty string. Return a set of strings; the adapter displays a JSON array and compares membership without imposing output order.
edgeCases: Empty string has one permutation
singleton
repeated characters under the bank extension.
Empty input returns the singleton set {""}; repeated characters yield distinct strings only, not repeated output entries.

explanation: Remove the last character and recursively permute the preceding substring. Insert that removed character at every position in each smaller permutation, storing results in an ordered std::set.
timeComplexity: O(n*n!*log(n!+1)) worst-case time for distinct characters: n! candidate strings cost O(n) to copy/insert characters, and each ordered-set insertion can make O(log(n!+1)) lexicographic comparisons costing O(n). This includes the ordered-set cost, unlike a hash-set bound.
spaceComplexity: O(n*n!) worst-case result and intermediate string storage, plus recursion depth O(n); repeated characters can reduce the number of distinct results.
attribution: Original EPI Practice implementation and explanation. Task identity and technical compatibility facts are attributed to Interview Cake; no course prose, examples, solution code or artwork are included. No affiliation is implied.
correctness: Deleting one occurrence of the last character from any full permutation leaves a permutation of the shorter input, which recursion produces. Reinserting it at every position therefore reconstructs every result; the ordered set removes duplicates.
walkthrough: For ab, recurse on a to obtain {a}. Insert the removed last character b at position 0 to get ba and at position 1 to get ab. The ordered set contains {ab,ba}. For empty input return {""}, allowing the first nonempty recursion level to insert its character. Return a set of strings; the adapter displays a JSON array and compares membership without imposing output order.
edgeCases: Empty string has one permutation
singleton
repeated characters under the bank extension.
Empty input returns the singleton set {""}; repeated characters yield distinct strings only, not repeated output entries.

explanation: Backtrack over a mutable character array. At each position, try each distinct remaining character once, swap it into that position, recurse, then undo the swap. A per-level chosen set skips duplicate choices.
timeComplexity: Expected O(n*n!) worst-case time: with distinct characters there are n! output strings, each constructed/hashed in O(n); all smaller recursion levels are dominated by this bound.
spaceComplexity: O(n*n!) worst-case output strings, plus O(n) character buffer/recursion depth and O(n²) worst-case total chosen-set entries retained along the recursion path.
attribution: Original EPI Practice implementation and explanation. Task identity and technical compatibility facts are attributed to Interview Cake; no course prose, examples, solution code or artwork are included. No affiliation is implied.
correctness: Positions before the recursion index form a fixed prefix and the suffix holds exactly its remaining multiset. Swapping each distinct suffix character into the next slot covers every possible next character once; undoing the swap restores the state for siblings. At the end every character has been used, and duplicate branches were excluded.
walkthrough: For ab at position 0, choose a and recurse on the remaining b to emit ab. Undo the swap, choose b from position 1, swap to ba, and emit ba. Restore ab after returning. For aa the chosen set skips the second identical choice at position 0, giving one result. Return a set of strings; the adapter displays a JSON array and compares membership without imposing output order.
edgeCases: Empty string has one permutation
singleton
repeated characters under the bank extension.
Empty input returns the singleton set {""}; repeated characters yield distinct strings only, not repeated output entries.

explanation: Maintain the already reversed prefix and detach one node at a time from the remaining suffix, pointing it back to the prefix.
timeComplexity: O(n) time: each of n nodes has its Next link rewritten once.
spaceComplexity: O(1) auxiliary space: current, saved next and previous references; no replacement nodes.
attribution: Original EPI Practice implementation and explanation. Task identity and technical compatibility facts are attributed to Interview Cake; no course prose, examples, solution code or artwork are included. No affiliation is implied.
correctness: The prefix always contains the original first nodes in reverse order, and the suffix is untouched. Moving its first node extends the invariant until no suffix remains.
walkthrough: For nodes 3 -> 8 -> 1, first set node 3.Next to null. Next point the original node 8 to node 3, then point the original node 1 to node 8. Return the original node holding 1. The resulting values are [1,8,3], with every payload still attached to its original object. The callable returns the new head of the same node objects. JSON displays the returned head’s value sequence; the adapter also checks original identities, payloads and reversed links.
edgeCases: Empty list
singleton identity
repeated values
old head becomes tail.
Empty input returns null; a singleton returns the same object. The old head becomes the tail with Next=null, even when payload values repeat.

explanation: Swap the leftmost and rightmost unprocessed characters, moving both boundaries inward.
timeComplexity: O(n) time: each inward swap fixes two characters, with at most ceil(n/2) swaps.
spaceComplexity: O(1) auxiliary space: two indices and a swap temporary; no new character buffer.
attribution: Original EPI Practice implementation and explanation. Task identity and technical compatibility facts are attributed to Interview Cake; no course prose, examples, solution code or artwork are included. No affiliation is implied.
correctness: Each swap places both boundary characters at their final reversed positions. The remaining middle interval is the same problem on fewer characters.
walkthrough: For the mutable characters of cloud, exchange c with d, then l with u; the middle o stays in place. The same array now contains duolc. No replacement array is returned. JSON encodes the mutable character array as one string. The callable returns void/None/undefined; expected is the same array’s content after mutation.
edgeCases: Empty array
singleton
even and odd lengths.
Empty and singleton arrays retain their identity and content. An odd-length center character stays unchanged.

explanation: Reverse the entire character array, then reverse the characters of each resulting word.
timeComplexity: O(n) time: one full reversal, one boundary scan, and word reversals whose total lengths sum to at most n.
spaceComplexity: O(1) auxiliary space: all reversals swap within the original mutable character array; only range indices are stored.
attribution: Original EPI Practice implementation and explanation. Task identity and technical compatibility facts are attributed to Interview Cake; no course prose, examples, solution code or artwork are included. No affiliation is implied.
correctness: The first reversal reverses word order and each word's letters. Reversing each word restores its spelling while leaving the new word order intact.
walkthrough: For foxes run fast, reversing all characters gives tsaf nur sexof. Reverse each space-delimited segment in that same array to restore the internal spelling, producing fast run foxes. Spaces remain separators and the array length is unchanged. JSON encodes the mutable character array as one string. The callable returns void/None/undefined; expected is the same array’s word-reversed content.
edgeCases: Empty/single word
unequal word lengths
two words.
Empty input stays empty. A single word is reversed twice and finishes unchanged; unequal word lengths need no extra storage.

explanation: Reverse the entire character array, then reverse the characters of each resulting word.
timeComplexity: O(n) time: one full reversal, one boundary scan, and word reversals whose total lengths sum to at most n.
spaceComplexity: O(1) auxiliary space: all reversals swap within the original mutable character array; only range indices are stored.
attribution: Original EPI Practice implementation and explanation. Task identity and technical compatibility facts are attributed to Interview Cake; no course prose, examples, solution code or artwork are included. No affiliation is implied.

explanation: Reject source outcomes 6 and 7; return every remaining outcome unchanged.
timeComplexity: Expected O(1) time: each attempt succeeds with probability 5/7, so the expected number of source calls is 7/5. There is no finite worst-case call bound.
spaceComplexity: O(1) auxiliary space: retain only the current draw, regardless of the number of rejected attempts.
attribution: Original EPI Practice implementation and explanation. Task identity and technical compatibility facts are attributed to Interview Cake; no course prose, examples, solution code or artwork are included. No affiliation is implied.
correctness: Each accepted source value has the same probability 1/7. Conditioning on acceptance gives probability 1/5 for each result; repeated independent attempts preserve that distribution.
walkthrough: With injected draws 6, 7, 3, reject 6 and 7 and return 3. In general each accepted source value 1..5 has the same source probability, so conditioning on acceptance gives probability 1/5. The judge output true denotes passed range, source-use and probability properties, not a fixed rolled value. Rand5 has no value arguments and returns one integer 1..5. JSON contains a judge-only forced Rand7 draw prefix; expected true denotes random-source/range/distribution checks, not the rolled integer.
edgeCases: Repeated rejections
every accepted value
do not map rejected outcomes modulo five.
Any number of 6/7 draws must be rejected; returning draw modulo five would bias outcomes. Every call uses fresh supplied randomness.

explanation: Combine two zero-based source draws into a uniform state in 0..24. Accept states below 21 and map each group of seven uniformly into 1..7.
timeComplexity: Expected O(1) time: an attempt succeeds with probability 21/25 and uses two source calls, for 50/21 expected calls. Worst-case attempts are unbounded.
spaceComplexity: O(1) auxiliary space: two draws and one encoded state, reused on every retry.
attribution: Original EPI Practice implementation and explanation. Task identity and technical compatibility facts are attributed to Interview Cake; no course prose, examples, solution code or artwork are included. No affiliation is implied.
correctness: Each pair is one of 25 equally likely states. Accepting 21 states leaves three representatives for each remainder modulo seven, so each result has conditional probability 1/7.
walkthrough: For injected draws 5,5,1,1, the first pair creates state (5-1)*5+(5-1)=24, which is rejected. The next pair creates state 0 and returns 1. Among accepted states 0..20, each remainder modulo seven occurs three times, giving probability 1/7 for each output. The displayed true reports the judge properties. Rand7 has no value arguments and returns one integer 1..7. JSON contains a judge-only forced Rand5 draw prefix; expected true denotes random-source/range/distribution checks, not the rolled integer.
edgeCases: Rejected top four states
repeated attempts
pair endpoints
no modulo bias from all 25 states.
States 21..24 must be rejected; taking all 25 states modulo seven would favor four outcomes. Repeated rejections must not cache a previous roll.

explanation: Keep a fixed 111-entry frequency table, running sum/count and cached extrema/mode. Each insertion updates these constant-size statistics.
timeComplexity: O(1) per insertion/getter: insertion changes one frequency bucket and a fixed number of cached statistics; getters read cached values.
spaceComplexity: O(1) persistent space: exactly 111 frequency slots plus count, sum, extrema and mode, independent of reading count.
attribution: Original EPI Practice implementation and explanation. Task identity and technical compatibility facts are attributed to Interview Cake; no course prose, examples, solution code or artwork are included. No affiliation is implied.
correctness: The frequency table counts every insertion. Extrema are updated against every new value; sum/count define the mean; updating the mode on a new largest frequency preserves a maximizing value.
walkthrough: Insert 4, 10 and 4. The minimum is 4, maximum 10, sum 18 and count 3, so the mean is 6. Frequency 4 is 2 while frequency 10 is 1, so GetMode returns 4. Repeating getters does not consume any reading. JSON supplies [operationNames,argumentLists] for one fresh TempTracker. Insert displays null; empty getters return null, means allow 1e-9 tolerance and any maximizing mode is valid.
edgeCases: Empty tracker
tied modes
repeated extrema
0 and 110
interleaved getters.
Empty getters return null. With readings 3 and 8, either mode is accepted; means use floating-point division and getters do not consume readings.

explanation: First detect an unbounded zero-weight type. Otherwise compute the best value for each capacity by considering the last positive-weight item selected.
timeComplexity: O(t*C+t+C+1) time: inspect t types for infinity, initialize C+1 cells, and test every type for each capacity 1..C.
spaceComplexity: O(C+1) auxiliary space: one best value per capacity, with no table indexed by item counts.
attribution: Original EPI Practice implementation and explanation. Task identity and technical compatibility facts are attributed to Interview Cake; no course prose, examples, solution code or artwork are included. No affiliation is implied.
correctness: For a bounded instance, an optimal nonempty selection has a final positive-weight item. Removing it leaves a feasible selection at the remaining capacity, so maximizing all such choices establishes the recurrence by induction.
walkthrough: For types [weight=3,value=7] and [weight=5,value=13] with capacity 11, choose one weight-5 item and two weight-3 items. Total weight is 11 and value is 13+7+7=27. Two weight-5 items yield only 26; three weight-3 items yield 21. The unbounded dynamic program reuses earlier capacity optima to find 27.
edgeCases: Zero-weight positive value
zero-weight zero value
empty types
zero capacity
values above 32 bits.
Any zero-weight positive-value type raises InfinityException even when capacity is zero. Zero-weight zero-value types are ignored; empty types produce value 0.

timeComplexity: O(t*C+t+C+1) time: inspect t types for infinity, initialize C+1 cells, and test every type for each capacity 1..C.
spaceComplexity: O(C+1) auxiliary space: one best value per capacity, with no table indexed by item counts.
attribution: Original EPI Practice implementation and explanation. Task identity and technical compatibility facts are attributed to Interview Cake; no course prose, examples, solution code or artwork are included. No affiliation is implied.
correctness: For a bounded instance, an optimal nonempty selection has a final positive-weight item. Removing it leaves a feasible selection at the remaining capacity, so maximizing all such choices establishes the recurrence by induction.
walkthrough: For types [weight=3,value=7] and [weight=5,value=13] with capacity 11, choose one weight-5 item and two weight-3 items. Total weight is 11 and value is 13+7+7=27. explanation: XOR all values. Each duplicated value cancels itself, leaving the unmatched one.
timeComplexity: O(n) time: perform one XOR per input entry.
spaceComplexity: O(1) auxiliary space: a single XOR accumulator and iteration state.
attribution: Original EPI Practice implementation and explanation. Task identity and technical compatibility facts are attributed to Interview Cake; no course prose, examples, solution code or artwork are included. No affiliation is implied.
correctness: XOR is associative and commutative, and x XOR x is zero. Paired values therefore cancel regardless of ordering, leaving the unique value.
walkthrough: For [14,3,14,8,3], XOR combines equal pairs to zero: 14^14=0 and 3^3=0. Since XOR is associative and commutative, the final accumulator equals 8, the only identifier without a cancelling partner.
edgeCases: Singleton
large nonconsecutive IDs
unique value at either end.
A singleton returns its value. Large or nonconsecutive IDs need no range-indexed storage; the exact once/twice multiplicity promise is essential.

explanation: Count occurrences in K+1 buckets, then emit each bucket from K down to zero.
timeComplexity: O(n+K+1) time: initialize and scan K+1 buckets, count n entries, then emit exactly n occurrences.
spaceComplexity: O(K+1) auxiliary count storage plus O(n) for the new output array.
attribution: Original EPI Practice implementation and explanation. Task identity and technical compatibility facts are attributed to Interview Cake; no course prose, examples, solution code or artwork are included. No affiliation is implied.
correctness: Each input occurrence increments exactly its score bucket. Emitting buckets in decreasing score order preserves multiplicity and produces the required ordering.
walkthrough: For scores [3,8,3,0,5] and K=8, the count table records one 8, one 5, two 3s and one 0. Reading counts from score 8 down to 0 emits [8,5,3,3,0] in a new array. Both occurrences of 3 are retained.
edgeCases: Empty input
repeated scores
unused top bucket.
K=0 permits only zeros, all retained; empty scores yield an empty new array even if K is positive.

explanation: Subtract n(n+1)/2 from the widened sum of all entries; the difference is the one extra occurrence.
timeComplexity: O(n) time: process the n+1 input entries; the range sum is constant-time arithmetic, or an additional n XOR operations in the XOR variants.
spaceComplexity: O(1) auxiliary space: scalar accumulator and range/loop variables, with no input mutation.
attribution: Original EPI Practice implementation and explanation. Task identity and technical compatibility facts are attributed to Interview Cake; no course prose, examples, solution code or artwork are included. No affiliation is implied.
correctness: The promised array contains one copy of each integer in 1..n plus one extra value x. Subtracting the exact required-range sum leaves x. Widen before multiplication to preserve arithmetic.
walkthrough: For [3,1,4,2,3], n is length-1=4. The expected sum 1+2+3+4 is 10, while the actual sum is 13. Their difference is 3, the duplicated value. Use widened arithmetic for the sum and formula before subtracting.
edgeCases: Minimum valid array
duplicate at endpoints of range
large n without sum overflow.
[1,1] returns 1. The promise includes every value 1..n and exactly one extra occurrence; the more general pigeonhole problem has a different contract.

timeComplexity: Expected O(n) time: tokenization, lowercase conversion and hashing examine O(n) total characters. The dictionary performs one expected constant-time update per token after hashing.
spaceComplexity: O(n) worst-case storage for dictionary keys and current token; an implementation that materializes all matches also stores O(n) matched characters.
attribution: Original EPI Practice implementation and explanation. Task identity and technical compatibility facts are attributed to Interview Cake; no course prose, examples, solution code or artwork are included. No affiliation is implied.
correctness: Each maximal sequence satisfying the disclosed token grammar is emitted once. Lowercasing maps permitted case variants to the same dictionary key, and one increment per token gives its occurrence count.
walkthrough: For "Owls fly; OWLS don't crawl. Fly-by owls!", punctuation ends tokens but internal apostrophes and letter-surrounded hyphens remain. Lowercasing combines Owls, OWLS and owls into count 3. The other keys are fly, don't, crawl and fly-by, each counted once under the disclosed bank policy. Construct WordCloudData from the input string and inspect WordsToCounts; the displayed dictionary is the exposed property, not a constructor return value. Dictionary order is irrelevant.

explanation: A repeated character is exactly a character whose presence flag was already set. Recording presence avoids comparing each character with every earlier character.
timeComplexity: O(n) time in the input length n.
spaceComplexity: O(128) = O(1) auxiliary space for the fixed ASCII alphabet.
attribution: Independently authored EPI Practice description, examples, implementation and explanation. Exercise reference: Cracking the Coding Interview, sixth edition, 1.1. No affiliation is implied.
correctness: Before each iteration, the flags represent exactly the characters in the processed prefix. An already-set flag supplies two occurrences and proves failure. Otherwise setting it preserves the invariant. Finishing without a repeat proves that every character occurs at most once.
walkthrough: For 'ink', the flags for i, n and k change from false to true, so the result is true. For 'level', l and e are recorded, then v; the next e already has a flag, so the result is false immediately.
edgeCases: Empty input is unique.
'aA' is unique; 'aa' is not.
Two spaces or two null characters are duplicates.

correctness: After processing first, each counter equals its frequency. While processing second, a counter equals the number of that character still available. A negative counter makes a permutation impossible. With equal lengths, consuming every character without a negative counter consumes the entire multiset, proving equivalence.
walkthrough: For 'a!ba' and 'ba!a', the first counts are a:2, !:1, b:1. Consuming b, a, !, a leaves all counts zero, so the result is true. Replacing the final a by b would make b's counter negative.
edgeCases: Multiplicity matters: 'aab' and 'abb' differ.
Case and whitespace are not normalized.
Both empty and unequal-length inputs are covered.

explanation: Each replacement expands one cell to three. Filling from the right keeps writes at or beyond the next unread character, so expansion cannot destroy text that still needs processing.
timeComplexity: O(n) time for the original prefix length n: one backward pass writes n + 2*s cells, where s <= n is the number of spaces. Exact capacity supplies the initial write position without a counting pass.
spaceComplexity: O(1) auxiliary space; the provided buffer is modified in place.
attribution: Independently authored EPI Practice description, examples, implementation and explanation. Exercise reference: Cracking the Coding Interview, sixth edition, 1.3. No affiliation is implied.
correctness: Initially the write position is the last cell of the required output. Before each backward step, the completed output suffix is correct and all unread original characters remain intact. Copying a nonspace consumes one input and one output cell; encoding a space consumes one input and three output cells. The remaining output length equals the remaining input length plus twice its space count, so writes never overwrite an earlier unread cell. Exhaustion produces exactly the encoded buffer.
walkthrough: For buffer ['g','o',' ','!','?','?'] and trueLength=4, write ! into cell 5, then write %,2,0 into cells 2..4, then copy o and g into cells 1 and 0. The final buffer is ['g','o','%','2','0','!']. Spare '?' values never become text.
edgeCases: Empty and space-free buffers.
Leading, trailing, adjacent, and all-space text.
Spare cells are not necessarily spaces; trueLength is authoritative.

explanation: Matching positions on opposite sides of a palindrome consume equal letters in pairs. Only a possible center may consume one unpaired letter, so at most one letter frequency may be odd.
timeComplexity: O(n) time, plus a fixed 26-letter scan.
spaceComplexity: O(128) = O(1) auxiliary space; only the 26 lowercase-letter slots are used.
attribution: Independently authored EPI Practice description, examples, implementation and explanation. Exercise reference: Cracking the Coding Interview, sixth edition, 1.4. No affiliation is implied.
correctness: After scanning, each of the 26 counts equals its retained letter's case-insensitive frequency. Necessity follows because all positions except a single center form equal pairs. For sufficiency, place half of each even part on either side in mirrored order and place the sole odd leftover, if present, at the center. Therefore at most one odd count is exactly the required condition.
walkthrough: For 'R!aCar', ignoring ! and folding case leaves racar. Counts are r:2, a:2, c:1, so c can be the center and the pairs can mirror around it. The answer is true. 'R!aCat' has three odd counts and returns false.
edgeCases: Punctuation-only and empty strings return true.
Case is folded only for ASCII English letters.
Two odd letter counts must fail even when spaces separate them.

explanation: The equal prefix needs no editing. At the first mismatch there is only one possible kind of repair given the two lengths: advance both pointers for replacement, or advance only the longer string for insertion/deletion. Any later mismatch requires a second edit.
timeComplexity: O(n + m) time in the input lengths.
spaceComplexity: O(1) auxiliary space, without allocating normalized or sliced copies.
attribution: Independently authored EPI Practice description, examples, implementation and explanation. Exercise reference: Cracking the Coding Interview, sixth edition, 1.5. No affiliation is implied.
correctness: Before a mismatch, both pointers delimit equal prefixes after the edits already used. A length difference above one is impossible to repair with one edit. With equal lengths, an insertion or deletion would leave unequal lengths, so the mismatch must be replaced. With unequal lengths, only skipping the longer string's next character can align the remaining suffixes. Accepting at most one such mismatch, including a possible final extra character, is necessary and sufficient.
walkthrough: For 'plane' and 'pane', p matches p. At l versus a, the lengths differ by one, so skip only l in the longer string. The remaining a,n,e match, giving true. For 'ab' and 'ba', replacing the first mismatch leaves a second mismatch, so the result is false.
edgeCases: Equal strings need zero edits.
Empty versus one character succeeds; empty versus two fails.
An extra character at either end is one edit; a transposition usually needs two.

explanation: A run's contribution is determined when its right boundary is reached. Collecting each contribution once preserves order and avoids repeatedly rescanning earlier characters. Comparing the final lengths prevents compression from expanding short runs.
timeComplexity: O(n) time to scan and build the candidate, where n is the input length. Counts have at most five digits under this bank's bound.
spaceComplexity: O(n) auxiliary/output-building space for the candidate.
attribution: Independently authored EPI Practice description, examples, implementation and explanation. Exercise reference: Cracking the Coding Interview, sixth edition, 1.6. No affiliation is implied.
correctness: At each run boundary the scan has found exactly one maximal contiguous block of the current letter. Appending its letter and length represents precisely that block; blocks partition the input, so concatenating their encodings produces the required candidate. Returning that candidate only for a strict length reduction implements the final selection rule, including ties.
walkthrough: For 'zzzzQQQQQx', the runs are z:4, Q:5, x:1. Their encodings form 'z4Q5x1', length 6 instead of 10, so it is returned. For 'zz', the candidate 'z2' ties length 2, so the original 'zz' is returned.
edgeCases: Empty string and one-letter input.
A length tie preserves the original.
Runs longer than nine need multidigit counts; uppercase and lowercase form separate runs.

def Compress(text: str) -> str:
    parts = []
    start = 0
    while start < len(text):
        end = start + 1
        while end < len(text) and text[end] == text[start]:
            end += 1
        parts.append(text[start])
        parts.append(str(end - start))
        start = end
    output = "".join(parts)
    return output if len(output) < len(text) else text

explanation: A clockwise rotation is a transpose followed by a reversal of each row. Transposing swaps row and column coordinates; row reversal changes the new column from r to n-1-r. Both steps use pairwise swaps on existing cells.
timeComplexity: O(n^2) time for an n by n matrix.
spaceComplexity: O(1) auxiliary space using individual swaps.
attribution: Independently authored EPI Practice description, examples, implementation and explanation. Exercise reference: Cracking the Coding Interview, sixth edition, 1.7. No affiliation is implied.
correctness: After transpose, the original cell (r,c) occupies (c,r). Reversing that row moves it to (c,n-1-r), exactly the required destination. Each transpose pair is swapped once using only positions above the diagonal; each row pair is swapped once. These are bijections, so no cell is lost or duplicated and row identities remain unchanged.
walkthrough: For [[2,5],[7,9]], transpose swaps 5 and 7 to get [[2,7],[5,9]]. Reversing each row produces [[7,2],[9,5]], the clockwise rotation. No row reference is replaced.
edgeCases: Empty and one-cell matrices.
Odd size leaves the center in place.
Repeated and negative values do not change coordinate rules.

explanation: Changing cells during discovery can mistake a newly written zero for an original zero. Record all affected row and column indices first, then clear cells in a separate pass using those records.
timeComplexity: O(r*c + r + c) time for r rows and c columns, including zero-column matrices; O(r*c) when both dimensions are positive.
spaceComplexity: O(r + c) auxiliary space for the row and column flags.
attribution: Independently authored EPI Practice description, examples, implementation and explanation. Exercise reference: Cracking the Coding Interview, sixth edition, 1.8. No affiliation is implied.
correctness: After the discovery pass, a row flag is true exactly when that original row contains a zero, and likewise for each column. The second pass writes zero if and only if either flag is true. Thus it clears exactly the union of originally affected rows and columns and leaves every other cell unchanged.
walkthrough: For [[4,0,6],[7,8,9]], discovery marks row 0 and column 1. Clearing those produces [[0,0,0],[7,0,9]]. The new zero at (1,1) does not mark row 1, so 7 and 9 survive.
edgeCases: No zero leaves the matrix unchanged; all zero stays all zero.
A single original zero clears only its row and column.
Rectangular, empty, single-row, single-column, and zero-column inputs.

explanation: If first is x+y and second is y+x, doubling first gives x+y+x+y, which contains y+x across the joining point. One search in the doubled string checks every split without testing each split separately.
timeComplexity: O(n + S(2n,n)) time, where S(h,p) is the runtime's substring-search cost. A conservative worst-case bound for an unspecified search implementation is O(n^2); do not assume a linear search guarantee in every language.
spaceComplexity: O(n) auxiliary space for the doubled string, plus any internal substring-search workspace.
attribution: Independently authored EPI Practice description, examples, implementation and explanation. Exercise reference: Cracking the Coding Interview, sixth edition, 1.9. No affiliation is implied.
correctness: Any rotation y+x appears in (x+y)+(x+y). Conversely, a length-n substring of first+first beginning in the first n positions consists of a suffix of first followed by its complementary prefix, so it is a rotation. Equality of positive lengths rules out shorter substrings and enforces the specified empty-input policy.
walkthrough: For 'orbit' and 'bitor', doubling gives 'orbitorbit'. Its length-five substring beginning at index 2 is 'bitor', so the answer is true. 'obrit' has the same characters but never occurs in the doubled text and is not a rotation.
edgeCases: Two empty strings return false; unequal lengths return false.
Identity and repeated-character rotations.
A rearrangement need not be a cyclic rotation.

explanation: A set answers whether the current value already has a retained occurrence. Only a duplicate must be bypassed; keeping a pointer to the last retained node makes that link change possible without searching backward.
timeComplexity: O(n) expected time with hash-set operations; pathological hashing can make the worst case O(n^2).
spaceComplexity: O(u) auxiliary space for u distinct values, at most O(n). No replacement list is allocated.
attribution: Independently authored EPI Practice description, examples, implementation and explanation. Exercise reference: Cracking the Coding Interview, sixth edition, 2.1. No affiliation is implied.
correctness: Before each step, the retained prefix contains exactly the first occurrences in the processed original prefix, in order. The set contains precisely those values. A new value extends both the set and retained prefix. An existing value is bypassed without advancing the retained predecessor. These cases preserve the invariant and, at exhaustion, retain exactly the required original nodes.
walkthrough: For original nodes [6,2,6,3,2], retain the first 6 and the first 2. Bypass the second 6, retain 3, then bypass the final 2. The reachable original nodes have indices [0,1,3] and values [6,2,3].
edgeCases: Empty and one-node lists.
All values equal keeps only the original head.
Nonadjacent duplicates and negative values.

explanation: Moving a lead pointer k links ahead creates a fixed k-link gap. Advancing both pointers together preserves that gap; when the lead falls off the end, the trailing pointer has exactly k nodes including itself left to the tail.
timeComplexity: O(n) time, including out-of-range k: the lead walk stops at null rather than performing k unchecked steps.
spaceComplexity: O(1) auxiliary space.
attribution: Independently authored EPI Practice description, examples, implementation and explanation. Exercise reference: Cracking the Coding Interview, sixth edition, 2.2. No affiliation is implied.
correctness: Nonpositive k cannot name a one-based position. If the lead reaches null before k advances, the list is too short. Otherwise the lead stays exactly k links ahead of the trailing pointer throughout the joint walk. At termination its position is one past the tail, so the trailing pointer is exactly kth from the tail and is an original node. No links or values are changed.
walkthrough: For [4,7,7,9] and k=2, advance the lead from index 0 to index 2. Joint steps move the pair to (3,1), then (null,2). Return the original node at index 2, whose value is 7; the equal-valued node at index 1 is not the answer.
edgeCases: Empty input and all nonpositive k return null.
k=1 selects the tail; k=n selects the head.
Repeated values require identity-sensitive grading.

explanation: Separate head/tail pointers for the two partitions let each node be appended to its proper side in constant time. Detach a node before appending it so old links cannot retain nodes in the wrong side or form cycles.
timeComplexity: O(n) time with one pass and constant-time tail appends.
spaceComplexity: O(1) auxiliary space; only a fixed number of node pointers is kept.
attribution: Independently authored EPI Practice description, examples, implementation and explanation. Exercise reference: Cracking the Coding Interview, sixth edition, 2.4. No affiliation is implied.
correctness: After each original node is processed, the two temporary lists contain disjoint processed original nodes, exactly partitioned by the comparison, with unchanged values. Appending the current node to the corresponding tail preserves this property. Joining the first list's tail to the second list's head places all smaller nodes before all remaining nodes and contains every original node exactly once. Empty sides are handled by returning the other head.

edgeCases: Empty input and either partition being empty.
All values equal to the pivot belong to the second side.
Repeated values require a node multiset/identity check, not only value counts.

explanation: Carry propagation starts at the units column. Reverse-order lists already expose that column first. Forward-order lists require access from their tails, so stacks of digits provide the same units-first processing without modifying the inputs. Each column contributes sum % 10 and a carry sum / 10 to the next column.
timeComplexity: O(n + m) time for operand lengths n and m, including a possible final carry.
spaceComplexity: O(1) auxiliary space in reverse-order mode, excluding the new result; O(n + m) auxiliary space for digit stacks in forward-order mode. The result has at most max(n,m)+1 nodes.
attribution: Independently authored EPI Practice description, examples, implementation and explanation. Exercise reference: Cracking the Coding Interview, sixth edition, 2.5. No affiliation is implied.
correctness: After processing k low-order columns, the emitted digits equal the low k decimal digits of the operand sum, and the carry is exactly the amount owed to the next column. Adding the next available digits (or zero for an exhausted operand) preserves this invariant by quotient/remainder division by ten. Processing a final carry completes the sum. Appending in reverse-order mode or prepending in forward-order mode places each generated digit in the declared output order. Every output node is newly allocated and input links are only read.
walkthrough: For forward-order [4,9] and [5,8], the operands are 49 and 58. The units column gives 9+8=17, so emit 7 with carry 1. The tens column gives 4+5+1=10, so emit 0 and carry 1. Prepending the final carry gives [1,0,7]. The same sum in reverse order uses [9,4] and [8,5] and returns [7,0,1].
edgeCases: Both empty; one empty; single-digit zero.
A carry propagating through all columns adds a leading digit.
Unequal lengths and both digit orders.
Input identity and disjoint newly allocated result nodes.

class LinkedListNode:
    def __init__(self, value: int, next: 'LinkedListNode | None' = None):
        self.Value, self.Next = value, next
def AddLists(
    first: LinkedListNode | None, second: LinkedListNode | None, mostSignificantFirst: bool
) -> LinkedListNode | None:
    if mostSignificantFirst:
        left, right = [], []
        current = first
        while current is not None:
            left.append(current.Value)
            current = current.Next
        current = second
        while current is not None:
            right.append(current.Value)
            current = current.Next
        result, carry = None, 0
        while left or right or carry:
            total = carry + (left.pop() if left else 0) + (right.pop() if right else 0)
            result = LinkedListNode(total % 10, result)
            carry = total // 10
        return result
    dummy = LinkedListNode(0)
    tail = dummy
    p, q, carry = first, second, 0
    while p is not None or q is not None or carry:
        total = carry
        if p is not None:
            total += p.Value
            p = p.Next
        if q is not None:
            total += q.Value
            q = q.Next
        tail.Next = LinkedListNode(total % 10)
        tail = tail.Next
        carry = total // 10
    return dummy.Next

explanation: Copying values into an auxiliary sequence gives direct access to mirrored positions without modifying singly linked links. Comparing only the first half tests each required mirrored pair once.
timeComplexity: O(n) time for traversal and mirrored comparisons.
spaceComplexity: O(n) auxiliary space for the copied values.
attribution: Independently authored EPI Practice description, examples, implementation and explanation. Exercise reference: Cracking the Coding Interview, sixth edition, 2.6. No affiliation is implied.
correctness: The auxiliary sequence is exactly the original head-to-tail value sequence because each node is read once in order. A sequence is a palindrome exactly when positions i and n-1-i are equal for every i below n/2. Rejecting the first unequal pair or accepting after all these comparisons implements that condition. The traversal never writes any node field, so every exit preserves the input.
walkthrough: For [3,8,1,8,3], copy the five values. Compare positions 0 and 4 (3=3), then positions 1 and 3 (8=8); the middle 1 needs no partner. Return true. Replacing the final value by 4 makes the first comparison fail, without changing a link.
edgeCases: Empty, one-node, even-length, and odd-length lists.
Repeated values alone do not guarantee a palindrome.
Early rejection must preserve all original links.

correctness: The auxiliary sequence is exactly the original head-to-tail value sequence because each node is read once in order. A sequence is a palindrome exactly when positions i and n-1-i are equal for every i below n/2. Rejecting the first unequal pair or accepting after all these comparisons implements that condition. The traversal never writes any node field, so every exit preserves the input.

edgeCases: Empty, one-node, even-length, and odd-length lists.
Repeated values alone do not guarantee a palindrome.
Early rejection must preserve all original links.

explanation: A pointer traversing first then second and another traversing second then first cover the same combined length. Switching heads after reaching null cancels any difference in private-prefix lengths without measuring them or changing a link.
timeComplexity: O(n + m) time for list lengths n and m.
spaceComplexity: O(1) auxiliary space.
attribution: Independently authored EPI Practice description, examples, implementation and explanation. Exercise reference: Cracking the Coding Interview, sixth edition, 2.7. No affiliation is implied.
correctness: Let private-prefix lengths be a and b and shared-suffix length c. If the pointers have not already met, their two-list routes reach the shared entry after the same a+b+c link advances and one head-switch step, so they meet at that entry, not merely an equal-valued node. Equal private-prefix lengths may make them meet earlier at that same entry. With no shared suffix, both routes have equal total length and end at null. Comparisons use object identity and the algorithm only reads links, so it returns exactly the first common node and preserves the lists.
walkthrough: For private prefixes [4,4] and [4], followed by the one shared suffix [9,2], the lists have lengths 4 and 3. Their first three 4-valued objects are separate. Head switching aligns the pointers at the shared 9 node, whose index in the first list is 2. Return that object, not either private 4 node.
edgeCases: Disjoint equal-valued lists must return null.
One or both null heads; identical heads; one head already inside the other list's suffix.
A one-node shared suffix and very unequal private-prefix lengths.

explanation: A fast pointer gains one position per step on a slow pointer inside a cycle, guaranteeing a collision. Their first collision is generally not the cycle entry. Resetting one pointer to the head and then advancing both at equal speed removes the prefix offset and locates the entry.
timeComplexity: O(n) time in the number of reachable original nodes: detection and entry alignment each use a linear number of advances.
spaceComplexity: O(1) auxiliary space.
attribution: Independently authored EPI Practice description, examples, implementation and explanation. Exercise reference: Cracking the Coding Interview, sixth edition, 2.8. No affiliation is implied.
correctness: If the fast pointer or its next link reaches null, there is no cycle. Otherwise let the noncyclic prefix have length mu and the cycle length lambda. At collision, slow has traveled t steps and fast 2t, so t is a multiple of lambda. The collision's cycle offset is therefore -mu modulo lambda. A pointer reset to the head reaches the entry after mu steps, while the other advances from that offset by mu and also reaches the entry. Before that point the reset pointer lies in the noncyclic prefix, so this is their first meeting. No field is written.
walkthrough: For values [6,1,6,4,8] and cycleIndex=2, the tail returns to the original second 6 node. With prefix length 2 and cycle length 3, the pointers first collide inside the cycle. Reset one to index 0 and take equal steps; after two steps both reach original index 2. Return that original object, despite the equal-valued head.
edgeCases: Empty and acyclic lists return null.
Self-loop, cycle at the head, and a long prefix before a short cycle.
Repeated payloads must not be mistaken for repeated node identities.

explanation: Giving stack s the disjoint interval starting at s*capacity makes its next free cell depend only on its size. Separate counters let a pop on one stack leave the other two stacks' payloads and tops unchanged.
timeComplexity: O(1) time per stack operation; construction takes O(capacity) time to initialize storage.
spaceComplexity: O(capacity) storage for the single 3*capacity payload array and constant-sized counters.
attribution: Independently authored EPI Practice description, examples, implementation and explanation. Exercise reference: Cracking the Coding Interview, sixth edition, 3.1. No affiliation is implied.
correctness: For each stack s, its occupied prefix of its reserved interval contains exactly its current bottom-to-top sequence, and size[s] is its length. Push writes at the next free offset and increases only that size. Pop reads the last occupied offset and decreases only that size; Peek reads without changing it. The intervals are disjoint, so these changes cannot affect another stack. Checks occur before writes, preserving state on every error.
walkthrough: With capacity 2, push 8 then 3 onto stack 0 and push 7 onto stack 2. Stack 0 is full and its Peek returns 3; stack 2's Peek returns 7. Popping stack 0 returns 3 and leaves 8 at its top. A push to a full stack fails even if stack 1 is empty, because this variant reserves fixed slots.
edgeCases: Capacity one; all three stacks used in interleaved order.
Full/empty errors followed by successful operations proving unchanged state.
Negative/too-large stack numbers; minimum and maximum integer payloads.

explanation: The minimum after popping a value is the minimum of the prefix that existed before that push. Store that prefix minimum beside each entry, so removing the top automatically restores the earlier minimum without rescanning.
timeComplexity: O(1) algorithmic time per operation under the usual constant-time node-allocation model. Destruction/garbage collection is separate from these stack operations.
spaceComplexity: O(n) live storage for n stack entries, each holding a value, prefix minimum and next link.
attribution: Independently authored EPI Practice description, examples, implementation and explanation. Exercise reference: Cracking the Coding Interview, sixth edition, 3.2. No affiliation is implied.
correctness: Each entry stores its own value and the minimum over that entry and every entry below it. A push computes the new minimum from the new value and the old top's stored minimum. A pop exposes the preceding entry, whose minimum already describes exactly the remaining stack. Therefore Peek, Pop and GetMin return the specified values, including repeated minima. An empty check precedes each access.
walkthrough: Push 9, then 4, then another 4. The stored prefix minima are 9,4,4. Popping one 4 leaves the previous entry's minimum 4; popping the second leaves 9. Keeping only a single uncounted minimum would lose that distinction.
edgeCases: Repeated minima must survive removal of only one copy.
Empty-stack failures do not change state.
All-negative values and both signed 32-bit endpoints.
