explanation: At the top-right remaining cell, everything below it is at least as large and everything to its left is no larger. A value above target rules out that entire column; a value below target rules out that entire row. This staircase walk removes one row or column per comparison.
timeComplexity: O(rows+columns) comparisons, since each step removes one row or column.
spaceComplexity: O(1) auxiliary row/column indices.
attribution: Independently authored EPI Practice description, examples, implementation and explanation. Exercise reference: Cracking the Coding Interview, sixth edition, 10.9. No affiliation is implied.
correctness: Initially every possible target position is in the full remaining rectangle. If its top-right value is larger than target, all values below in that column are also too large, so removing the column is safe. If smaller, all remaining values in that row are too small, so removing the row is safe. Equality returns a verified coordinate. This invariant preserves every possible match until the rectangle empties, proving the [-1,-1] result then means absence.
walkthrough: For [[1,4,7],[2,5,8],[3,6,9]] and target 6, begin at 7 and move left to 4. Move down to 5, then down to 6, returning [2,1]. Flattened binary search would be invalid because 7 at the end of row 0 exceeds 2 at the start of row 1.
edgeCases: Empty dimensions, one row or column, target outside the value range.
Duplicates, signed endpoints and row ranges that overlap.

explanation: A search-tree node can cache how many tracked occurrences lie in its left subtree. Route equal inserted values left, so that count also includes earlier/later duplicates beneath an equal node. A rank query accumulates entire left subtrees and ancestor nodes only when moving right; finding the queried value adds its left count without counting that node itself.
timeComplexity: O(h) per Track/GetRank for tree height h. The actual BST is not balanced: worst-case h equals the number of tracked occurrences; do not claim guaranteed logarithmic time.
spaceComplexity: O(t) stored nodes after t tracked occurrences and O(1) auxiliary iterative traversal space, excluding the returned transcript results.
attribution: Independently authored EPI Practice description, examples, implementation and explanation. Exercise reference: Cracking the Coding Interview, sixth edition, 10.10. No affiliation is implied.
correctness: Every insertion preserves the BST rule left<=node<right and increments a node's left count exactly when the new occurrence enters that left subtree. During a query, the accumulated count contains exactly the smaller/equal occurrences already skipped on right turns. At equality, every left-subtree occurrence is <=value, and the current node is the one excluded occurrence, so accumulated+leftCount is the required rank. If traversal reaches no matching node, the value is absent and -1 is returned regardless of the partial accumulated count. Iterative traversal avoids recursion-depth failures on a skewed stream.
walkthrough: Track 5,1,4,4. Sorted tracked values are [1,4,4,5]. GetRank(4) returns 2: one 1 and the OTHER 4 count, while one queried 4 is excluded. GetRank(2) returns -1 even though its insertion position would be 1. A new tracker begins empty.
edgeCases: Query before any Track and query an absent interior value.
Repeated equal values count other copies; negative and signed-endpoint values.
Ascending/descending streams create skewed trees but not recursive stack overflow.

explanation: For each odd position, put the largest value among it and its existing neighbors at that position. It then dominates both neighbors. If the left neighbor is swapped, it receives a value no greater than its old value, so it cannot break the previous peak. This permits a single local pass instead of sorting.
timeComplexity: O(n) time for one constant-work step per odd position; the C++ returned copy is also O(n).
spaceComplexity: O(1) auxiliary rearrangement storage, excluding the C++ returned value copy.
attribution: Independently authored EPI Practice description, examples, implementation and explanation. Exercise reference: Cracking the Coding Interview, sixth edition, 10.11. No affiliation is implied.
correctness: After processing an odd position, it is at least both adjacent values by construction. The only cell shared with the preceding processed triple is its left neighbor. If that neighbor is chosen as the new peak, the displaced center is no larger than the old neighbor, so the previous peak still dominates it; other swaps do not change that shared neighbor. Induction therefore preserves all earlier peaks. Every odd position is processed, so the final array has the full alternating pattern. Swaps alone preserve every original occurrence.
walkthrough: Starting with [1,2,3,4,5], put 3 at odd index 1 by swapping it with 2, giving [1,3,2,4,5]. Then swap 5 into odd index 3, yielding [1,3,2,5,4]. Both peaks dominate their neighbors; the middle valley 2 is below both 3 and 5.
edgeCases: Empty, singleton, equal values and two-element arrays.
Signed extremes must not be confused with out-of-bounds sentinels.
Multiple valid outputs are accepted, but all input occurrences must remain.

explanation: XOR removes a repeated operand: x xor x is zero and x xor zero is x. The first assignment stores the combined information of both inputs. XORing that combination with the old second recovers the original first, then XORing it with the recovered first recovers the original second. No addition/subtraction overflow is required.
timeComplexity: O(1) fixed-width XOR operations.
spaceComplexity: O(1) auxiliary storage; no swap temporary, plus the two-integer output.
attribution: Independently authored EPI Practice description, examples, implementation and explanation. Exercise reference: Cracking the Coding Interview, sixth edition, 16.1. No affiliation is implied.
correctness: Let the original values be a and b. After the first assignment, first=a xor b and second=b. The second assignment makes second=(a xor b) xor b=a. The third makes first=(a xor b) xor a=b. XOR associativity and cancellation therefore exchange the two values exactly. This remains valid for equal values and all signed bit patterns because the two variables are distinct locations.
walkthrough: With first=9 and second=4, the assignments produce first=13, then second=9, then first=4. The returned pair is [4,9]. If both values are 7, the intermediate first becomes zero but the following assignments recover [7,7].
edgeCases: Equal inputs, zeros and negative values.
Both signed endpoints; arithmetic overflow must not break exchange.

def SwapWithoutTemporary(first: int, second: int) -> list[int]:
    first ^= second
    second ^= first
    first ^= second
    return [first, second]

explanation: Many queries share the same book. Normalize case once per occurrence and accumulate counts in a dictionary, then normalize and look up each query. This pays for reading the book once instead of once per requested word.
timeComplexity: Expected O(B+Q) character work for B book characters and Q query characters, assuming expected constant dictionary access per bounded-length key. Hash-table collisions can worsen this bound.
spaceComplexity: O(D*L+q) storage for D distinct normalized book words of maximum length L and q returned counts; query normalization uses O(L) temporary storage.
attribution: Independently authored EPI Practice description, examples, implementation and explanation. Exercise reference: Cracking the Coding Interview, sixth edition, 16.2. No affiliation is implied.
correctness: After processing any prefix of book, the dictionary count for each normalized word equals its occurrences in that prefix: inserting a new normalized key starts its count and every later occurrence increments it once. Induction gives exact counts for the entire book. A normalized query identifies precisely its case-insensitive equivalence class; lookup returns that count, or zero when no occurrence created its key. Appending answers in query order preserves repeated queries and their positions.
walkthrough: For book=[Red,blue,RED,green] and queries=[red,BLUE,missing,Red], normalized counts are red:2, blue:1, green:1. The answers are [2,1,0,2]. Red and RED contribute to the same count; the repeated red query does not consume a book occurrence.
edgeCases: Empty book or query array; all queries absent.
Mixed case, repeated book words and repeated queries.

explanation: Many queries share the same book. Normalize case once per occurrence and accumulate counts in a dictionary, then normalize and look up each query. This pays for reading the book once instead of once per requested word.
timeComplexity: Expected O(B+Q) character work for B book characters and Q query characters, assuming expected constant dictionary access per bounded-length key. Hash-table collisions can worsen this bound.
spaceComplexity: O(D*L+q) storage for D distinct normalized book words of maximum length L and q returned counts; query normalization uses O(L) temporary storage.
attribution: Independently authored EPI Practice description, examples, implementation and explanation. Exercise reference: Cracking the Coding Interview, sixth edition, 16.2. No affiliation is implied.
correctness: After processing any prefix of book, the dictionary count for each normalized word equals its occurrences in that prefix: inserting a new normalized key starts its count and every later occurrence increments it once. Induction gives exact counts for the entire book. A normalized query identifies precisely its case-insensitive equivalence class; lookup returns that count, or zero when no occurrence created its key. Appending answers in query order preserves repeated queries and their positions.
walkthrough: For book=[Red,blue,RED,green] and queries=[red,BLUE,missing,Red], normalized counts are red:2, blue:1, green:1. The answers are [2,1,0,2]. Red and RED contribute to the same count; the repeated red query does not consume a book occurrence.
edgeCases: Empty book or query array; all queries absent.
Mixed case, repeated book words and repeated queries.

explanation: A winning line can only belong to one of a finite set: n rows, n columns and two full diagonals. For each candidate, take its first cell as the proposed player and verify the remaining cells; an empty first cell immediately disqualifies the line. This covers the generic square-board follow-up without assuming the board is always 3 by 3.
timeComplexity: O(n^2) time: examine at most 2n+2 lines of length n.
spaceComplexity: O(1) auxiliary space; no board copy or history is needed.
attribution: Independently authored EPI Practice description, examples, implementation and explanation. Exercise reference: Cracking the Coding Interview, sixth edition, 16.4. No affiliation is implied.
correctness: A candidate is reported only when its first cell is nonzero and every cell in that full line equals it, so every reported player has a genuine winning line. Conversely every allowed winning line appears among the examined rows, columns or two diagonals and therefore will be detected. The at-most-one-winner promise makes early return safe even if that player has several winning lines. If no candidate succeeds, neither player has a win and zero is correct.
walkthrough: For [[1,0,2],[0,1,2],[0,0,1]], no row or column is complete, but the main diagonal contains 1,1,1, so player 1 wins. Three adjacent 1 cells on one row of a 4 by 4 board would not be a complete winning line.
edgeCases: Empty and one-cell boards, all-empty board, full board without a winner.
Both diagonal directions, full columns, and nonwinning partial lines in larger boards.

explanation: A decimal trailing zero consumes one factor 2 and one factor 5. Factorials supply more twos than fives, so only the number of fives matters. Multiples of 25 contribute a second five, multiples of 125 a third, and so on. Repeatedly dividing n by five counts each contribution without growing a power that might overflow.
timeComplexity: O(log_5(n+1)) integer divisions and additions; zero takes constant time.
spaceComplexity: O(1) auxiliary space; the factorial and powers of five are never stored.
attribution: Independently authored EPI Practice description, examples, implementation and explanation. Exercise reference: Cracking the Coding Interview, sixth edition, 16.5. No affiliation is implied.
correctness: For every exponent k>=1, floor(n/5^k) counts exactly the factors among 1..n supplying at least k copies of five. A factor containing t fives appears in exactly t such counts, so their sum is precisely the total five exponent. Twos are at least as numerous, hence this exponent equals the number of factors of ten. Replacing n by floor(n/5) at each iteration produces these successive quotients. Once it reaches zero, no higher power contributes.
walkthrough: For 25!, multiples 5,10,15,20,25 supply five copies of five, and 25 supplies one extra. The successive quotients are 5,1,0, so the result is 6. Counting multiples of five only would incorrectly return 5.
edgeCases: Zero and numbers below five.
Just below, at and above powers of five; the maximum signed input.

explanation: Sorted copies expose the closest cross-array neighbors without checking every pair. At current values a and b, moving the larger value can only keep or increase the gap while the smaller stays fixed. Record their difference, then advance the smaller side to seek a closer value.
timeComplexity: O(n log(n+1)+m log(m+1)) sorting time plus O(n+m) pointer advances.
spaceComplexity: O(n+m) for the two private sorted copies; library sorting workspace is bounded by this storage.
attribution: Independently authored EPI Practice description, examples, implementation and explanation. Exercise reference: Cracking the Coding Interview, sixth edition, 16.6. No affiliation is implied.
correctness: Consider current sorted values a<=b. Every not-yet-visited value on the second side is at least b, so none can improve the recorded b-a while a stays fixed. Discarding a is safe. The symmetric argument applies when b<a. Every discarded value has therefore been paired with its best remaining candidate, and any candidates skipped earlier were already bounded by an earlier recorded difference. The least recorded difference is the global minimum. Equal values certify the optimal lower bound zero. Empty input has no cross-array pair and uses the explicit -1 convention.
walkthrough: For first=[10,1,20] and second=[14,5], sort copies to [1,10,20] and [5,14]. Record gaps 4 (1,5), 5 (10,5), 4 (10,14), and 6 (20,14), returning 4. For [-2147483648] and [2147483647], the exact answer is 4294967295 rather than an overflowing signed value.
edgeCases: Either input empty, duplicates and a shared value.
Signed endpoints and differences above 2147483647.

explanation: The sign of first-second decides which input is larger only when subtraction cannot overflow. If signs differ, the nonnegative input is larger regardless of the wrapped difference. If signs agree, the difference fits signed range and its sign is reliable. Combine those two choices as zero/one selectors instead of branching.
timeComplexity: O(1) fixed-width arithmetic and bit operations.
spaceComplexity: O(1) auxiliary scalar storage.
attribution: Independently authored EPI Practice description, examples, implementation and explanation. Exercise reference: Cracking the Coding Interview, sixth edition, 16.7. No affiliation is implied.
correctness: Let a and b be bits indicating negative inputs, and d indicate a negative 32-bit difference. When a xor b is one, choose first exactly when a is zero. When their xor is zero, choose first exactly when d is zero; equal inputs may choose first. These two cases are disjoint and exhaustive. The computed selector is therefore zero or one and selects precisely a maximum input. A mask derived from the selector copies the chosen input bits. C++ computes the difference in uint32_t and converts the selected exact signed operand arithmetically, avoiding signed-overflow and implementation-defined unsigned-to-signed conversion.
walkthrough: For first=-2147483648 and second=2147483647, subtraction wraps to the positive bit pattern 1. Its sign alone would select the wrong input. The argument signs differ, so the selector instead chooses the nonnegative second input. For 9 and 4, signs agree and the positive difference correctly chooses 9.
edgeCases: Opposite signed endpoints, equal values, zero and negatives.
A subtraction that wraps must not influence the opposite-sign choice.

code:
def MaximumWithoutComparison(first: int, second: int) -> int:
    negative_first = (first >> 31) & 1
    negative_second = (second >> 31) & 1
    negative_difference = ((first - second) & 0xFFFFFFFF) >> 31
    different = negative_first ^ negative_second
    choose_first = different * (negative_first ^ 1) + (different ^ 1) * (negative_difference ^ 1)
    mask = -choose_first
    return (first & mask) | (second & ~mask)

The computed selector is therefore zero or one and selects precisely a maximum input. A mask derived from the selector copies the chosen input bits. C++ computes the difference in uint32_t and converts the selected exact signed operand arithmetically, avoiding signed-overflow and implementation-defined unsigned-to-signed conversion.
walkthrough: For first=-2147483648 and second=2147483647, subtraction wraps to the positive bit pattern 1. Its sign alone would select the wrong input. The argument signs differ, so the selector instead chooses the nonnegative second input. For 9 and 4, signs agree and the positive difference correctly chooses 9.
edgeCases: Opposite signed endpoints, equal values, zero and negatives.
A subtraction that wraps must not influence the opposite-sign choice.

def EnglishInteger(value: int) -> str:
    if value == 0:
        return "Zero"
    small = [
        "Zero",
        "One",
        "Two",
        "Three",
        "Four",
        "Five",
        "Six",
        "Seven",
        "Eight",
        "Nine",
        "Ten",
        "Eleven",
        "Twelve",
        "Thirteen",
        "Fourteen",
        "Fifteen",
        "Sixteen",
        "Seventeen",
        "Eighteen",
        "Nineteen",
    ]
    tens = ["", "", "Twenty", "Thirty", "Forty", "Fifty", "Sixty", "Seventy", "Eighty", "Ninety"]
    scales = ["", "Thousand", "Million", "Billion"]
    magnitude = abs(value)
    groups = []
    scale = 0
    while magnitude:
        chunk = magnitude % 1000
        if chunk:
            words = []
            if chunk >= 100:
                words.extend([small[chunk // 100], "Hundred"])
                chunk %= 100
            if chunk >= 20:
                words.append(tens[chunk // 10])
                chunk %= 10
            if chunk:
                words.append(small[chunk])
            if scale:
                words.append(scales[scale])
            groups.append(" ".join(words))
        magnitude //= 1000
        scale += 1
    return ("Negative " if value < 0 else "") + " ".join(reversed(groups))

explanation: Subtraction is addition of the opposite value. Build that opposite by moving the operand toward zero one unit at a time while accumulating the same movement. Multiplication is repeated addition, and division counts how many whole positive divisor magnitudes fit. Choose the signed addend or quotient step up front so no large product needs a second unit-by-unit sign reversal.
timeComplexity: O(abs(first)+abs(second)+1) worst-case time on this bounded integer domain: sign reversal and repeated addition/removal use at most proportional unit/count loops. Division has at most abs(first) iterations.
spaceComplexity: O(1) auxiliary scalar storage; no lookup table or arithmetic helper bypass is used.
attribution: Independently authored EPI Practice description, examples, implementation and explanation. Exercise reference: Cracking the Coding Interview, sixth edition, 16.9. No affiliation is implied.
correctness: In sign reversal, current+(-accumulated) remains the original value: each unit added to current is also added to accumulated. Reaching current=0 therefore leaves the exact opposite original operand. Adding that opposite proves subtraction. Multiplication adds the correctly signed first operand exactly abs(second) times, so the result has the required magnitude and sign. Division maintains abs(first)=consumedMagnitude+remaining with remaining nonnegative; each accepted divisor removal adds one correctly signed quotient unit. Termination occurs exactly when another whole divisor would exceed the remainder, proving truncation toward zero. Bounds justify all intermediate sums.
walkthrough: For divide(-7,3), obtain magnitude 7 by adding +1 seven times to -7 and accumulating 7. The divisor magnitude is 3 and its additive opposite is -3. Remainders 7->4->1 permit two removals; a third would be negative. The quotient step is -1 because signs differ, so return -2. For multiply(-4,-3), use addend 4 three times, returning 12.
edgeCases: Zero dividend/factors, same and opposite signs, divisor magnitudes exceeding the dividend.
Truncation toward zero and admitted positive/negative endpoints.
Division by zero and unsupported operation names are outside the stated input domain.

def AdditionOnlyArithmetic(first: int, second: int, operation: str) -> int:
    def opposite(value):
        step = 1 if value < 0 else -1
        result = 0
        while value != 0:
            value += step
            result += step
        return result

    if operation == "subtract":
        return first + opposite(second)
    if operation == "multiply":
        count = opposite(second) if second < 0 else second
        addend = opposite(first) if second < 0 else first
        result = 0
        while count > 0:
            result += addend
            count += -1
        return result
    remaining = opposite(first) if first < 0 else first
    divisor = opposite(second) if second < 0 else second
    remove = opposite(divisor)
    step = 1 if (first < 0) == (second < 0) else -1
    result = 0
    while remaining + remove >= 0:
        remaining += remove
        result += step
    return result

explanation: A birth increases the population starting in its own year. A death decreases it only in the following year because the death year is included. Recording those changes and taking a prefix sum counts all lifetimes without visiting every person in every year. Scan years in increasing order and update the winner only on a strictly larger population to retain the earliest tie.
timeComplexity: O(p+Y) time for p people and Y=101 admitted years, hence O(p+1) for this fixed domain.
spaceComplexity: O(Y) change counters including a death-after-2000 sentinel; Y is fixed at 101.
attribution: Independently authored EPI Practice description, examples, implementation and explanation. Exercise reference: Cracking the Coding Interview, sixth edition, 16.10. No affiliation is implied.
correctness: Each person contributes +1 at birth and -1 at death+1. Their contribution to the running sum is consequently one exactly during their inclusive lifetime and zero elsewhere. Summing all contributions yields the exact living population in every scanned year. The running best records the largest population seen and changes its year only when that count increases. Increasing-year order therefore chooses the earliest global maximizer, including 1900 for the all-zero empty case.
walkthrough: For [[1900,1901],[1901,1902],[1902,1902]], populations in 1900,1901,1902 are 1,2,2. The first person still counts in 1901 and the third counts in 1902. The maximum is tied, so return 1901 rather than the last tied year.
edgeCases: No people, same-year lifetimes, duplicate date rows.
Birth coinciding with another death; earliest tied year and the 2000 endpoint.

def MostPopulatedYear(people: list[list[int]]) -> int:
    changes = [0] * 102
    for birth, death in people:
        changes[birth - 1900] += 1
        changes[death - 1900 + 1] -= 1
    alive = 0
    best = 0
    answer = 1900
    for offset in range(101):
        alive += changes[offset]
        if alive > best:
            best = alive
            answer = 1900 + offset
    return answer

explanation: Only the number of long planks affects the total; the ordering of those planks does not. For k long planks, total length is planks*shorter+k*(longer-shorter). Enumerating k from zero through planks covers all choices without exploring 2^planks arrangements. Equal plank lengths collapse all counts to one answer.
timeComplexity: O(planks+1) time when lengths differ, matching output size; O(1) when equal.
spaceComplexity: O(1) auxiliary space excluding the returned O(planks+1) integer values, or one value for equal lengths.
attribution: Independently authored EPI Practice description, examples, implementation and explanation. Exercise reference: Cracking the Coding Interview, sixth edition, 16.11. No affiliation is implied.
correctness: Every board uses a unique count k of long planks between zero and planks, so its total has the stated formula. Conversely every such k is feasible by choosing k long planks and the rest short. When longer>shorter, increasing k strictly increases the total, proving the generated list is sorted and contains no duplicates. When lengths agree, all choices yield the single emitted total. The k=0 empty-board case yields zero.
walkthrough: For 3 planks of lengths 2 and 5, choose 0,1,2,3 long planks to get 6,9,12,15. Short-long-short and long-short-short both have length 9 and appear once. With equal lengths 2 and 2, only 6 is returned.
edgeCases: Zero planks, equal lengths, one plank.
Maximum count and lengths, without integer overflow or duplicate totals.

explanation: Fix one input point as an anchor. Every different point on one line through it has the same reduced direction after dividing by gcd and normalizing orientation. Count those direction groups and add coincident occurrences to every group. Repeat for every anchor, keeping the highest score. This stores only one anchor's groups rather than every pairwise line object.
timeComplexity: Expected O(n^2*log(C+1)) arithmetic/hash work for coordinate-difference bound C=2000, hence expected O(n^2) in this fixed domain. Hash collisions can worsen the bound.
spaceComplexity: O(n) direction counts for one anchor plus constant-size returned coefficients.
attribution: Independently authored EPI Practice description, examples, implementation and explanation. Exercise reference: Cracking the Coding Interview, sixth edition, 16.14. No affiliation is implied.
correctness: For a fixed anchor, normalized directions agree exactly for points on the same undirected line through it; gcd reduction avoids fractional/vertical special guesses. Coincident occurrences lie on every such line and must be added to each group. For any maximum line containing distinct locations, its earliest original anchor has all its other occurrences among the later points, so that anchor's group reaches the full optimum count. No reported group can exceed the true optimum because its coefficients define a real line through all counted occurrences. All-coincident input is covered by the explicit vertical fallback. Integer cross-products give exact membership without tolerance ambiguity.
walkthrough: For [[0,0],[1,1],[2,2],[0,1]], anchoring at [0,0] groups [1,1] and [2,2] under reduced direction (1,1). That line has three occurrences and equation x-y=0, so [1,-1,0] is valid. Vertical lines use B=0; repeated [0,0] occurrences add to every line through that anchor.
edgeCases: No points, one point and all coincident points.
Vertical/horizontal lines, negative slopes, duplicate occurrences and multiple optimal lines.
Nearly parallel rational slopes must remain distinct; exact integer arithmetic replaces an epsilon guess.

explanation: Reserve exact matches first so their occurrences cannot be reused. Among the unmatched positions, only remaining color multiplicities matter: each unmatched guess can consume one occurrence of its color if available. A frequency table implements this matching without pairing the same secret slot twice.
timeComplexity: O(1) for the fixed four slots; two passes and a fixed four-color table.
spaceComplexity: O(1) auxiliary space and a two-integer result.
attribution: Independently authored EPI Practice description, examples, implementation and explanation. Exercise reference: Cracking the Coding Interview, sixth edition, 16.15. No affiliation is implied.
correctness: The first pass counts every exact match and excludes both its occurrences from later matching. For each other secret slot, it adds one available occurrence of that color. The second pass ignores hit slots and consumes an available matching color for each unmatched guess. For every color this creates exactly the minimum of its unmatched guess and secret multiplicities, which is the greatest possible one-to-one matching count. Colors are disjoint, so their sum is the pseudo-hit count.
walkthrough: For guess GGRR and secret RGBY, slot 1 is a G hit. Remaining secret colors are R,B,Y; remaining guesses are G,R,R. Only one R can consume the single remaining R, so the score is [1,1], not [1,2].
edgeCases: All hits, no matches, all one color.
Repeated guessed colors cannot consume one unmatched secret occurrence twice.

explanation: Scanning left to right, any value below the largest earlier value is too far right and must lie inside the sorting window. Its last occurrence of such a violation fixes the right endpoint. Symmetrically, a value above the smallest later value is too far left; scanning backward locates the left endpoint. This avoids sorting a full copy just to find mismatches.
timeComplexity: O(n) time for two scans.
spaceComplexity: O(1) auxiliary storage, excluding the two-integer output.
attribution: Independently authored EPI Practice description, examples, implementation and explanation. Exercise reference: Cracking the Coding Interview, sixth edition, 16.16. No affiliation is implied.
correctness: At each forward position, the running maximum equals the maximum of the prefix. A value smaller than that maximum cannot be fixed without including its position, so the last such position is a necessary right bound. The reverse argument makes the first position above its suffix minimum a necessary left bound. Outside those bounds, values are ordered consistently with all preceding or following values. Sorting the enclosed region therefore removes all cross-order violations and makes the whole array nondecreasing. Since neither bound can be excluded, the resulting window is shortest. No forward violation means no inversion and hence an already sorted array.
walkthrough: For [1,2,4,3,3,5], the running maximum becomes 4 at index 2; indices 3 and 4 are below it, so right=4. Scanning backward, the suffix minimum is 3 when index 2 is reached, giving left=2. Sorting indices 2..4 produces [1,2,3,3,4,5].
edgeCases: Empty, singleton, already sorted, all equal.
Reverse order, duplicates around both endpoints, signed extremes.

explanation: For any next element, a best suffix either extends a nonnegative previous suffix or starts afresh. A negative running prefix can never improve a future sum, so discard it. Retain a separate best-so-far total so ending a promising sequence does not lose its result.
timeComplexity: O(n) time in one scan.
spaceComplexity: O(1) auxiliary scalar storage.
attribution: Independently authored EPI Practice description, examples, implementation and explanation. Exercise reference: Cracking the Coding Interview, sixth edition, 16.17. No affiliation is implied.
correctness: After processing a prefix, running is the maximum of zero and the sums of all suffixes of that prefix. Appending the next value extends every nonempty candidate suffix; taking max(0,running+value) also permits the empty suffix and subsumes starting with this value alone. Induction preserves that invariant. Every contiguous sequence ends at some position, so updating best with every running value finds the greatest of all sequence sums, including the empty sequence.
walkthrough: For [2,-8,3,-2,4,-10], running totals after discarding negative suffixes are 2,0,3,1,5,0. The best is 5 from [3,-2,4]. Adding all positive elements would incorrectly return 9 because those positions are not contiguous.
edgeCases: Empty and all-negative inputs return zero.
Zeros, all-positive input, a best interval strictly inside the array.

code:
def MaximumContiguousSum(values: list[int]) -> int:
    running = 0
    best = 0
    for value in values:
        running = max(0, running + value)
        best = max(best, running)
    return best

correctness: After processing a prefix, running is the maximum of zero and the sums of all suffixes of that prefix. Appending the next value extends every nonempty candidate suffix; taking max(0,running+value) also permits the empty suffix and subsumes starting with this value alone. Induction preserves that invariant. Every contiguous sequence ends at some position, so updating best with every running value finds the greatest of all sequence sums, including the empty sequence.

explanation: If a appears ca times and b appears cb times, candidate replacement lengths must satisfy ca*la+cb*lb=text.length. Enumerate one used length, derive the other, and verify every occurrence against the first substring assigned to its symbol. This avoids enumerating all possible replacement strings independently.
timeComplexity: O((n+1)*(n+p+1)) conservative time for text length n and pattern length p: at most n+1 length choices, with O(n+p) slice/comparison work each.
spaceComplexity: O(n) replacement-slice storage plus O(1) counters; no expanded candidate string is built.
attribution: Independently authored EPI Practice description, examples, implementation and explanation. Exercise reference: Cracking the Coding Interview, sixth edition, 16.18. No affiliation is implied.
correctness: Every valid substitution has nonnegative lengths satisfying the total-length equation, so its length pair is among those tested. For a tested pair, scan pattern from left to right and assign a symbol the text slice at its first occurrence; later occurrences must equal that slice. This enforces consistent replacements and advances by exactly the chosen length. The total-length equation ensures the final offset is the text end. Thus any accepted pair defines a valid full substitution, and the pair of any valid substitution passes verification. Empty/unused-symbol cases follow the explicit zero-length and full-consumption rules.
walkthrough: For pattern=abba and text=redbluebluered, lengths a=3 and b=4 assign red at the first a and blue at the first b. The second b matches blue and the last a matches red, consuming all text, so return true. For pattern=ab and text=x, a may be empty and b=x; distinct nonempty replacements are not required.
edgeCases: Empty pattern/text and a pattern using only one symbol.
Empty or equal replacement strings, mismatched repeated symbols and unmatched trailing text.

explanation: Start a search only at an unvisited water cell, mark it on discovery, and count every water cell reached through eight-neighbor steps. Every such search consumes exactly one connected component. Separate visited flags preserve the elevation input; marking before pushing avoids counting a water cell twice. Sorting the component counts provides the bank's deterministic output order without merging equal-sized ponds.
timeComplexity: O(rows*columns + p*log(p+1)) time for the scan/search and sorting p pond sizes. Each cell and its eight neighbors are checked a constant number of times.
spaceComplexity: O(rows*columns) visited flags and worst-case work stack, excluding the p returned sizes.
attribution: Independently authored EPI Practice description, examples, implementation and explanation. Exercise reference: Cracking the Coding Interview, sixth edition, 16.19. No affiliation is implied.
correctness: The search starts within one pond, and each discovered water neighbor is connected to a reached water cell, so it remains in that same pond. Every water cell in the pond has a water path from the start; induction along that path shows it is eventually reached. Marking at discovery gives exactly one count per cell. The outer scan starts no later search in an already visited component, while every other pond eventually supplies an unvisited starting cell. Thus the recorded sizes include every pond once. Sorting changes only their order, not multiplicity, and the elevation grid is never changed.
walkthrough: In [[0,1,0],[1,0,1],[0,1,0]], the center water cell touches every corner diagonally. All five zeros are therefore one pond, so return [5]. Four-neighbor searches would incorrectly report five ponds of size one.
edgeCases: No water, all water, empty dimensions.
Diagonal-only connections, separate equal-sized ponds, and boundary/corner cells.

explanation: Each dictionary word has exactly one keypad encoding. Check only words of the requested length and compare each letter's digit with the query. This avoids generating all exponential letter combinations, most of which might not be dictionary words.
timeComplexity: O(W+T) time for W dictionary entries and at most T examined word characters; each entry is visited once and length-mismatched words need no character scan.
spaceComplexity: O(R) returned word references/copies for R matches, plus a constant 26-entry mapping and scalar loop indices; C++ returned strings also copy their character contents.
attribution: Independently authored EPI Practice description, examples, implementation and explanation. Exercise reference: Cracking the Coding Interview, sixth edition, 16.20. No affiliation is implied.
correctness: For a word of the right length, the fixed keypad table maps each letter to its unique allowed digit. Equality at every position holds exactly when that word is one valid spelling of the query; a length mismatch or any differing mapped digit makes it impossible. Visiting every dictionary entry therefore returns all and only matches. Appending during the original-order scan preserves ordering and duplicates. Since no letter maps to 0 or 1 and words are nonempty, the explicit no-match cases follow automatically.
walkthrough: For digits=8733 and dictionary=[tree,used,true,tree], tree maps t->8,r->7,e->3,e->3 and used maps u->8,s->7,e->3,d->3. true maps to 8783, so the result is [tree,used,tree], retaining the repeated entry.
edgeCases: Empty dictionary/query, digits 0/1 and words of a different length.
Four-letter keypad groups pqrs/wxyz, duplicate dictionary entries and no matches.

explanation: Writing the new sums as S1-a+b and S2-b+a gives 2*(a-b)=S1-S2. An odd total difference is impossible. Otherwise, for each a in first, the only possible b is a-(S1-S2)/2; a hash set of second values answers membership without testing every pair.
timeComplexity: Expected O(n+m) time for sums, building the membership set and one scan; hash collisions can worsen the bound.
spaceComplexity: O(m) membership storage plus a constant-size returned pair.
attribution: Independently authored EPI Practice description, examples, implementation and explanation. Exercise reference: Cracking the Coding Interview, sixth edition, 16.21. No affiliation is implied.
correctness: Any valid exchange satisfies the derived equation, so an odd sum difference rules out all possibilities. For an even difference, every scanned a has exactly one required b. A set membership hit proves both values occur and substitution into the equation proves the new sums agree. Conversely, every valid exchange has a first-array occurrence that the scan visits and its required second value is in the set, so a valid exchange cannot be missed. Scanning original first order and returning the first hit implements the tie rule. No hit proves absence.
walkthrough: For first=[4,1,2,1,1,2] (sum 11) and second=[3,6,3,3] (sum 15), the half-difference is -2. The first value 4 requires second value 6, which exists, so return [4,6]. The hypothetical new sums are both 13; the supplied arrays stay unchanged.
edgeCases: Empty inputs, odd total difference, equal sums but no shared value.
Multiple exchanges, repeated values, negative totals and signed endpoints.

code:
def LangtonBoard(steps: int) -> list[str]:
    black = set()
    row = column = direction = 0
    min_row = max_row = min_column = max_column = 0
    dr, dc = [0, 1, 0, -1], [1, 0, -1, 0]
    for _ in range(steps):
        position = (row, column)
        if position in black:
            direction = (direction + 3) % 4
            black.remove(position)
        else:
            direction = (direction + 1) % 4
            black.add(position)
        row += dr[direction]
        column += dc[direction]
        min_row, max_row = min(min_row, row), max(max_row, row)
        min_column, max_column = min(min_column, column), max(max_column, column)
    result = []
    for r in range(min_row, max_row + 1):
        line = []
        for c in range(min_column, max_column + 1):
            line.append(
                "RDLU"[direction] if (r, c) == (row, column) else "#" if (r, c) in black else "."
            )
        result.append("".join(line))
    return result

explanation: Sort a private copy and inspect its smallest and largest remaining values. If their sum is too small, the smallest cannot pair with anything; if too large, the largest cannot pair with anything. On equality, consume both occurrences. Complementary value classes cannot compete with other classes, so using a valid pair cannot reduce the eventual pair count.
timeComplexity: O(n log(n+1)) time for sorting plus O(n) endpoint steps.
spaceComplexity: O(n) for the private sorted copy and O(p) returned pairs, p<=floor(n/2).
attribution: Independently authored EPI Practice description, examples, implementation and explanation. Exercise reference: Cracking the Coding Interview, sixth edition, 16.24. No affiliation is implied.
correctness: For sorted endpoints a<=b, a+b<target means no remaining partner is large enough for a; discarding a loses no valid pair. Similarly a+b>target rules out every remaining partner for b. On equality, a can pair only with value b and b only with value a. Taking that pair reduces the available counts of those complementary classes by one each (or by two for equal values), achieving the maximum possible count for that class. Repeating these safe steps produces a maximum number of disjoint pairs. Left endpoints never decrease, so normalized pairs are already in lexicographic order; all are drawn from distinct consumed occurrences.
walkthrough: For values=[1,1,2,2,3,3] and target 4, the sorted endpoints yield [1,3], then another [1,3], then [2,2]. All six occurrences are used once. With only three 2s and target 4, return one [2,2], leaving one unused; returning three index pairs would reuse occurrences.
edgeCases: No pair, singleton, duplicate pairs and odd equal-value multiplicity.
Negative targets, zero and signed endpoints requiring widened sums.

explanation: Lookup needs a key index, while eviction needs a recency order that supports removing an arbitrary accessed entry and adding it at the most-recent end. A dictionary plus doubly linked list provides both. Languages with an ordered-map facility can use its equivalent movement operations; an ordinary successful lookup alone does not necessarily refresh recency. C# indexes LinkedListNode<(int Key,string Text)> objects in a Dictionary. Removing and re-adding the same node at the list tail refreshes recency without a linear key search. Replacing a value updates that node rather than creating a duplicate entry.
timeComplexity: Expected O(1) per Get/Set under conventional hash/ordered-map implementations; hash collisions can worsen access. JavaScript Map specifies average sublinear access rather than a strict constant-time guarantee. Value copying costs O(value.length) where applicable.
spaceComplexity: O(capacity) entries plus stored key/value data; the returned transcript uses O(operationCount) slots. Values are at most 20 characters.
attribution: Independently authored EPI Practice description, examples, implementation and explanation. Exercise reference: Cracking the Coding Interview, sixth edition, 16.25. No affiliation is implied.
correctness: Maintain exactly one indexed entry for each cached key and an order from least to most recently used. A missing Get changes neither structure. An existing Get or Set moves its one entry to the most-recent end; Set also stores the new value. A new Set appends one entry and, only when capacity is exceeded, removes the oldest entry from both index and order. These updates preserve one-to-one membership, correct values and recency after every operation. Thus each eviction selects precisely the least recently used surviving key, and every Get returns the current value or null exactly when absent.
walkthrough: With capacity 2, Set(1,A), Set(2,B) orders keys [1,2]. Get(1) returns A and changes order to [2,1]. Set(3,C) evicts 2, leaving [1,3]. Get(2) returns null without refreshing anything; Get(1) still returns A. With capacity 1, Set(7,"") followed by Get(7) returns an empty string, not null.
edgeCases: Capacity one, absent Get, repeated Set of an existing key and successful Get recency refresh.

explanation: Lookup needs a key index, while eviction needs a recency order that supports removing an arbitrary accessed entry and adding it at the most-recent end. A dictionary plus doubly linked list provides both. Languages with an ordered-map facility can use its equivalent movement operations; an ordinary successful lookup alone does not necessarily refresh recency. Java LinkedHashMap is constructed with accessOrder=true. Its successful get and put refresh order; after a new insertion exceeds capacity, the first key iterator entry is the least recently used and is removed. Default insertion-order LinkedHashMap would not implement Get refresh.

spaceComplexity: O(capacity) entries plus stored key/value data; the returned transcript uses O(operationCount) slots. Values are at most 20 characters.

explanation: XOR gives the sum bits that need no carry. AND identifies positions where both operands contain a one, and shifting those positions left produces pending carries. Repeat with the carry-free result and pending carries until no carries remain. Fixed-width masking is essential in Python, where negative integers do not automatically have 32-bit width.
timeComplexity: O(w) bit-operation rounds for a w-bit word, at most 32 here; therefore bounded O(1) for this fixed-width callable.
spaceComplexity: O(1) auxiliary scalar storage; iterative implementations use no recursion stack.
attribution: Independently authored EPI Practice description, examples, implementation and explanation. Exercise reference: Cracking the Coding Interview, sixth edition, 17.1. No affiliation is implied.
correctness: For each bit position, XOR contributes the low sum bit and the shifted AND contributes its carry into the next position. Replacing the operands by those two patterns preserves their total modulo 2^32. Each pending carry moves left, so after at most 32 rounds none remains within the word. The remaining pattern is therefore the required modular sum. C#/Java/JavaScript naturally observe the fixed-width pattern; Python masks each carry and reinterprets the final sign. C++ uses unsigned shifts and a fixed-width byte copy for the signed result, avoiding undefined signed left shift or narrowing.
walkthrough: For 5 and 3, the first XOR is 6 and the pending carry is 2. Next they become 4 and 4, then 0 and 8, then 8 and 0. The returned result is 8. For -1 and 1, the carry propagates through the whole word and is discarded above bit 31, leaving zero.
edgeCases: Zero, equal values, negative values and long carry chains.
Both signed endpoints and sums that wrap across either endpoint.

explanation: Give each letter weight +1 and each digit weight -1. An interval has equal category counts exactly when its endpoint prefix balances agree. For each balance, keep its earliest prefix position; using a later occurrence could only shorten a future interval. A dense offset array suffices because every balance is between -n and n.
timeComplexity: O(n) time to scan characters and initialize the 2n+1 balance slots.
spaceComplexity: O(n) auxiliary first-occurrence slots, plus two returned indices.
attribution: Independently authored EPI Practice description, examples, implementation and explanation. Exercise reference: Cracking the Coding Interview, sixth edition, 17.5. No affiliation is implied.
correctness: The difference of two prefix balances is the letter count minus digit count in the enclosed substring, so equality is equivalent to balance. At each end position, pairing with the earliest prior equal balance gives the longest balanced substring ending there. Every possible end is examined, so the longest of these candidates is globally optimal. End positions increase; keeping the first equal-length optimum also keeps the smallest start. Initial balance zero at prefix index -1 admits intervals starting at zero. No repeated balance means no qualifying nonempty interval.
walkthrough: For A1B2C the successive balances after each character are 1,0,1,0,1. Balance zero at index 3 matches the initial zero at -1, giving [0,3] (A1B2), length four. Balance one at index 4 gives [1,4], also length four; the earlier start wins.
edgeCases: Empty input and a single category.
An optimum starting at zero, mixed letter cases, equal-length tied windows.

def LongestLettersDigits(text: str) -> list[int]:
    n = len(text)
    first = [-2] * (2 * n + 1)
    first[n] = -1
    balance = best = 0
    start = end = -1
    for index, char in enumerate(text):
        balance += -1 if "0" <= char <= "9" else 1
        slot = balance + n
        if first[slot] == -2:
            first[slot] = index
        elif index - first[slot] > best:
            best = index - first[slot]
            start, end = first[slot] + 1, index
    return [start, end]

explanation: At one decimal place of weight p, the digit pattern repeats every 10p numbers. Every complete block contributes p twos in that place. The final partial block contributes zero, a partial run, or a full p depending on whether the current digit is below, equal to, or above two. Add the independent counts for all places.
timeComplexity: O(log_10(n+1)) decimal places; zero takes constant time.
spaceComplexity: O(1) auxiliary scalar storage.
attribution: Independently authored EPI Practice description, examples, implementation and explanation. Exercise reference: Cracking the Coding Interview, sixth edition, 17.6. No affiliation is implied.
correctness: Write n as high*(10p)+digit*p+low with 0<=low<p. The high complete blocks contribute high*p. If digit<2, the final block has not reached its run of twos. If digit=2, that run includes low+1 numbers; if digit>2, it includes all p. Thus the formula counts precisely all occurrences at that position among 0..n. Summing over positions counts every occurrence once, including both positions in 22. Higher leading positions contribute nothing. Wide intermediates prevent overflow of 10p at the billions place.
walkthrough: Through 25, the ones place contributes 3 occurrences, in 2,12,22. The tens place contributes 6, in 20..25. The total is 9; 22 intentionally contributes to both place counts. Through 1 the answer is zero.
edgeCases: Zero, 2, 12, 22, and boundaries around powers of ten.
Current digit below/equal/above two; the largest signed input needs wide place intermediates.

def CountDigitTwos(n: int) -> int:
    total = 0
    place = 1
    while place <= n:
        high = n // (place * 10)
        digit = (n // place) % 10
        low = n % place
        total += high * place
        if digit == 2:
            total += low + 1
        elif digit > 2:
            total += place
        place *= 10
    return total

explanation: Synonymous names are connected components of an undirected graph. Build adjacency from the given pairs, visit each name once, and sum its frequency into that component. Mark names when adding them to the work queue so repeated/cyclic synonym declarations cannot double-count a name.
timeComplexity: O(n+e) traversal time for n names and e listed synonym pairs, using direct index adjacency; duplicate pair contributions are still visited only as listed edges.
spaceComplexity: O(n+e) adjacency, visited/work queue and returned group rows.
attribution: Independently authored EPI Practice description, examples, implementation and explanation. Exercise reference: Cracking the Coding Interview, sixth edition, 17.7. No affiliation is implied.
correctness: A graph path is exactly a chain of synonym declarations, so connected components coincide with the required equivalence groups. Starting at an unvisited name, traversal reaches every and only name in its component. Marking on discovery makes each name enter once, so adding its frequency once yields the exact component total despite duplicate/self edges. Later starts skip visited components, producing one row per group. The starting name is an original member and therefore a valid representative; no lexical or insertion-order representative is required.
walkthrough: For names=[John,Jon,Johnny,Chris], frequencies=[10,3,0,4] and pairs [[0,1],[1,2]], the first three spellings form one group totaling 13, including the zero-count bridge Johnny. Chris remains a separate group with 4. [[0,13],[3,4]] and [[2,13],[3,4]] are both valid results.
edgeCases: No names, isolated names and all-zero frequencies.
Transitive synonym chains, zero-frequency bridge spellings, duplicate/reverse/self pairs.
Any original representative and arbitrary group-row order are accepted.

explanation: Sort original indices by height, then use dynamic programming over possible final people. A shorter/lighter predecessor can extend a valid tower; retaining a predecessor index reconstructs an actual maximum tower rather than only its length. Checking BOTH strict comparisons keeps equal dimensions from forming invalid links. C# sorts an int[] of original indices and compares dimensions with CompareTo, so the supplied person rows never move. The predecessor walk collects those original indices before reversing them; returning sorted-array positions would identify different people.
timeComplexity: O(n^2) dynamic-programming comparisons after O(n log(n+1)) private index sorting.
spaceComplexity: O(n) index, length, predecessor and returned-index storage.
attribution: Independently authored EPI Practice description, examples, implementation and explanation. Exercise reference: Cracking the Coding Interview, sixth edition, 17.8. No affiliation is implied.
correctness: Every predecessor of a person in a valid top-to-bottom tower has smaller height and therefore occurs earlier in the private sorted order. For each person, the recurrence takes one plus the largest valid predecessor tower length, or one if none exists. Induction over that order proves each recorded length is optimal among towers ending there. The global best endpoint consequently has maximum possible length. Following its recorded predecessor links reconstructs only strict height/weight links, and reversing them yields top-to-bottom original indices. Private index sorting leaves caller rows unchanged.
walkthrough: For people=[[65,100],[70,150],[56,90]], the sorted index order is [2,0,1]. Each person can follow the previous one, so return [2,0,1]. For [[60,100],[60,90]], only one person can be used despite the different weights, because heights must also increase strictly.
edgeCases: Empty/single person, duplicate rows and ties in either dimension.
A best tower using neither original input order nor every person; arbitrary maximum-tower ties.

explanation: Merge the increasing sequences obtained by multiplying already generated values by 3,5 and 7. One pointer per factor identifies its smallest candidate not yet emitted. Pick the minimum candidate, then advance EVERY pointer that produced it so a value such as 15 is not emitted twice.
timeComplexity: O(k+1) time: one constant-size minimum and three possible pointer advances per generated value.
spaceComplexity: O(k+1) stored sequence values and three pointers.
attribution: Independently authored EPI Practice description, examples, implementation and explanation. Exercise reference: Cracking the Coding Interview, sixth edition, 17.9. No affiliation is implied.
correctness: Initially the generated list contains only 1. Every other permitted number is a smaller permitted number times at least one of 3,5,7. Each pointer skips exactly candidates already emitted; hence the minimum of their next candidates is the smallest permitted value still missing. Appending it maintains increasing complete order. Advancing all equal producers removes duplicate histories without removing a distinct value. By induction list[k] is exactly the requested zero-indexed value.
walkthrough: After 1, candidates 3,5,7 give 3, then 5, then 7, then 9. The value 15 is produced both as 3*5 and 5*3. Both responsible pointers advance when 15 is appended, so the next output is 21 rather than another 15. Therefore index 5 returns 15.
edgeCases: Index zero, first few values, and duplicate-producing products such as 15 and 105.
Largest admitted index with no signed multiplication overflow.

explanation: Cancel pairs of different values: a strict majority cannot be eliminated by these cancellations, because each canceled majority occurrence removes a nonmajority occurrence too. Keep a candidate and an unmatched balance instead of storing all counts. Cancellation produces only a candidate, so a second pass must verify that it actually exceeds half the original length.
timeComplexity: O(n) time for cancellation and verification scans.
spaceComplexity: O(1) auxiliary scalar storage plus a result containing at most one integer.
attribution: Independently authored EPI Practice description, examples, implementation and explanation. Exercise reference: Cracking the Coding Interview, sixth edition, 17.10. No affiliation is implied.
correctness: When the balance reaches zero, all processed values can be partitioned into unlike canceled pairs. A positive balance represents that many uncanceled copies of the candidate. Removing unlike pairs preserves the identity of any strict majority, so if one exists it is the final candidate. The second pass counts that candidate in the original array and returns it only if its count exceeds floor(n/2), proving both soundness and completeness. With no majority, including empty input, verification returns the empty collection.
walkthrough: For [2,1,2,3,2], cancellation leaves candidate 2. Verification finds three copies among five values, so return [2]. For [1,2,3], a candidate still survives the first pass, but its single occurrence is not a majority, so return [].
edgeCases: Empty input, a singleton, exactly-half frequency, no majority.
A genuine -1 majority, signed endpoints, and a candidate requiring second-pass rejection.

explanation: Remember the most recent position of each requested word. When one appears, its closest partner among all earlier opposite-word occurrences is the latest such occurrence. Updating the best distance at those encounters finds every possible closest cross-word boundary without storing all positions.
timeComplexity: O(n*L) worst-case character comparison work for n tokens and maximum word length L; O(n) token comparisons.
spaceComplexity: O(1) auxiliary index/count storage.
attribution: Independently authored EPI Practice description, examples, implementation and explanation. Exercise reference: Cracking the Coding Interview, sixth edition, 17.11. No affiliation is implied.
correctness: For any occurrence at index i, every earlier opposite-word index j has distance i-j. This distance is smallest for the largest such j, which is exactly the remembered last position. Every pair has a later endpoint; when that endpoint is scanned, the algorithm considers a pair at least as close. Taking the least of these candidate distances therefore finds the global minimum. Only actual occurrences update remembered positions, so every candidate is valid. If either word never occurs, no candidate exists and the explicit -1 result is correct.
walkthrough: For words=[red,x,blue,red,y,blue], first=red and second=blue, the encounter at index 2 yields distance 2 from red at 0. The red at index 3 is only 1 away from blue at 2, improving the best to 1. The final blue is 2 away from red at 3, so return 1, not zero intervening words.
edgeCases: Empty text, one or both words absent.
Adjacent targets, repeated runs and the closest pair appearing late.

explanation: A prefix either ends with one unrecognized character, costing one extra, or with a recognized dictionary word, costing nothing beyond the best preceding prefix. correctness: Every produced tokenization ends in either a recognized word or an unrecognized segment. explanation: The largest retained value is the only one that a new smaller candidate needs to displace. A max heap exposes it immediately while keeping just k values. Values at least as large as the root cannot improve the retained multiset. Extracting largest-first in reverse positions, or sorting the final heap values, produces the required ascending output. C# PriorityQueue normally removes the lowest priority. A reversed Comparer makes the largest retained value leave first; CompareTo avoids overflowing a subtraction at signed endpoints. Dequeue into output positions from right to left to obtain ascending order.
timeComplexity: O(n*log(k+1) + k*log(k+1)) time including heap updates and ordered output; k=0 takes O(1).
spaceComplexity: O(k) heap/result storage and no input-sized copy when k is small.
attribution: Independently authored EPI Practice description, examples, implementation and explanation. Exercise reference: Cracking the Coding Interview, sixth edition, 17.14. No affiliation is implied.
correctness: After the first k values, the heap contains exactly their k-smallest multiset. Inductively, a new value no smaller than the root leaves that multiset optimal; a smaller value replaces one largest retained occurrence, yielding precisely the k smallest values of the extended prefix. Equal values are ordinary separate occurrences and are neither deduplicated nor overcounted. At the end the retained multiset is the required answer, and output ordering changes only its order. The zero-k branch returns before accessing a heap root.
walkthrough: For [5,1,5,-2,3] and k=3, the initial heap retains [5,1,5]. Reading -2 displaces one 5; reading 3 displaces the remaining 5. The retained values are -2,1,3, returned in that order. For k=4, one 5 must remain: duplicates are not a set.
edgeCases: k=0, k equal to input size, empty input.
Repeated boundary values, negative values, and signed extremes without comparator-subtraction overflow.

explanation: For each candidate, use prefix dynamic programming to record how many dictionary components can spell each reachable prefix. A valid final prefix needs at least two components, so the candidate's own dictionary membership cannot falsely qualify it. A set permits component membership checks; comparing successful candidates by length and then lexicographic order resolves the output unambiguously.
timeComplexity: Expected O(W*L^3) character work for W candidate entries of maximum length L: O(L^2) substrings per candidate, each costing up to O(L) copying/hashing. Hash collisions can worsen membership costs.
spaceComplexity: O(D*L) dictionary storage plus O(L) DP and substring workspace per candidate, for D distinct words; the input is not sorted or mutated.
attribution: Independently authored EPI Practice description, examples, implementation and explanation. Exercise reference: Cracking the Coding Interview, sixth edition, 17.15. No affiliation is implied.
correctness: Let dp[i] be the largest number of components spelling the first i characters, or -1 when unreachable, with dp[0]=0. Every transition appends a nonempty dictionary substring to a reachable prefix, so it creates a valid decomposition. Conversely, removing the last component of any valid decomposition leaves a shorter reachable prefix; induction ensures the transition for that last component is considered. Thus dp[length]>=2 holds exactly for candidates with the required decomposition. Keeping the longest successful word and the smallest lexicographic word on a length tie produces the specified global choice. Repeated component use is allowed because membership is not consumed.
walkthrough: For [cat,dog,catdog,dogcat,catcatdog], catdog and dogcat each have two components. catcatdog has three: cat+cat+dog, so its length 9 beats their length 6 and it is returned. For [cat,dog,catdog,dogcat], the equal-length tie selects catdog. A dictionary containing only cat has no qualifying word.
edgeCases: No composed word, repeated dictionary entries and a word that equals only itself.
Repeated component reuse, multiple decompositions and equal-length lexical ties.

explanation: For each prefix, an optimal choice either skips its final appointment or accepts it and therefore skips its neighbor. Only the best totals for the preceding one and two prefixes are needed. Rolling those two totals gives the full optimum without storing a table or enumerating all subsets.
timeComplexity: O(n) time in one prefix scan.
spaceComplexity: O(1) auxiliary storage for two preceding optima and a temporary update.
attribution: Independently authored EPI Practice description, examples, implementation and explanation. Exercise reference: Cracking the Coding Interview, sixth edition, 17.16. No affiliation is implied.
correctness: Let B(i) be the best total using the first i appointments, with B(0)=0. If appointment i-1 is skipped, the optimum is B(i-1). If accepted, the remaining choices are exactly a valid optimum for the first i-2 appointments, giving duration[i-1]+B(i-2). These cases are exhaustive, and their maximum is B(i). The two rolling variables hold those earlier prefix optima before each step; updating after computing the maximum maintains the invariant and returns the full-sequence optimum.
walkthrough: For [30,15,60,75,45,15,15,45], prefix optima are 30,30,90,105,135,135,150,180. One optimal choice takes indices 0,2,4,7, totaling 30+60+45+45=180. Choosing the larger appointment from each adjacent pair independently would not enforce constraints across pair boundaries.
edgeCases: Empty input, zero durations, one appointment.

code:
def MaximumMassageMinutes(appointments: list[int]) -> int:
    one_back = two_back = 0
    for duration in appointments:
        current = max(one_back, duration + two_back)
        two_back = one_back
        one_back = current
    return one_back
explanation: For each prefix, an optimal choice either skips its final appointment or accepts it and therefore skips its neighbor. Only the best totals for the preceding one and two prefixes are needed. Rolling those two totals gives the full optimum without storing a table or enumerating all subsets.
timeComplexity: O(n) time in one prefix scan.
spaceComplexity: O(1) auxiliary storage for two preceding optima and a temporary update.

explanation: The direct baseline tests each legal start position independently for each query. Bounding starts by text.length-pattern.length prevents overreads, while advancing by one retains overlaps. Returning rows rather than a map preserves the order and multiplicity of the supplied query list.
timeComplexity: O(P+sum(max(0,n-m+1)*(m+1))) worst-case time over P patterns of lengths m and text length n; this is the direct baseline, not a trie-optimized search.
spaceComplexity: O(K+P+L) for K returned positions, P result rows and at most L temporary substring characters; constant comparison indices beyond the output in versions using direct character comparison.
attribution: Independently authored EPI Practice description, examples, implementation and explanation. Exercise reference: Cracking the Coding Interview, sixth edition, 17.17. No affiliation is implied.
correctness: A legal occurrence of a pattern of length m must start at one of the positions 0 through n-m, and the loop examines each exactly once. Character-by-character equality (or equivalent exact substring comparison) accepts precisely the windows spelling that pattern, so no occurrence is missed or invented. Increasing start order yields increasing output positions and includes overlaps. For m=0, each of the n+1 legal windows is empty, giving the stated boundary convention. An outer loop over patterns preserves every query position, including duplicates.
walkthrough: For text=ababa and patterns=[aba,ba,z,""], aba starts at [0,2], ba at [1,3], and z has no match. The empty pattern row is [0,1,2,3,4,5]. The two aba occurrences overlap at index 2; moving by pattern length would miss one.
edgeCases: Empty text/pattern, missing pattern and a pattern longer than text.

explanation: Expand the right edge until the window contains all required values, then shrink its left edge while that remains true. Track only required-value frequencies and how many required values are still absent. Unneeded values can be skipped at the left, and duplicate needed values can be removed until the last occurrence would disappear.
timeComplexity: Expected O(big.length + small.length) time with hash-map operations; each window edge advances at most big.length times.
spaceComplexity: O(small.length) auxiliary map entries, plus the two-index output.
attribution: Independently authored EPI Practice description, examples, implementation and explanation. Exercise reference: Cracking the Coding Interview, sixth edition, 17.18. No affiliation is implied.
correctness: The frequency map always counts each required value inside the current window; missing equals the number with zero count. Thus missing=0 exactly characterizes a covering window. For each right edge, removing left entries until coverage would fail examines the shortest feasible window ending there. No discarded earlier left edge could give a shorter future window than the surviving one. Every right edge is processed, so the best recorded candidate is globally shortest. Strictly shorter updates during increasing right order preserve the earliest start among ties.
walkthrough: For big=[7,5,9,1,5,9,1] and small=[1,5,9], indices 1..3 contain 5,9,1 and cover the target in length three. Later windows 2..4 and 3..5 have the same length, so [1,3] remains the answer. Matching the target in its supplied order would incorrectly reject valid windows.
edgeCases: Empty target, empty big array, missing target value.
Target values in a different order, redundant occurrences, and equal-length ties.

explanation: XOR the full range and the supplied entries: present values cancel, leaving a xor b for the missing pair. Because a and b differ, some bit is set in that XOR. Partition both the full range and input by one such bit; the two missing values land in different groups, and all present values cancel within their own groups.
timeComplexity: O(n) time for full-range and input XOR scans.
spaceComplexity: O(1) auxiliary scalar storage, excluding the two-value output.
attribution: Independently authored EPI Practice description, examples, implementation and explanation. Exercise reference: Cracking the Coding Interview, sixth edition, 17.19. No affiliation is implied.
correctness: Each present value appears twice in the full/input XOR and cancels, leaving exactly the two missing values. A set bit of their XOR means one missing value has that bit and the other does not. Repeating XOR separately for the two bit groups therefore leaves one missing value in each accumulator. These are the complete missing pair; ordering them changes no membership. All values and the selected low bit fit the admitted signed range, so no square sums or floating-point roots can overflow or round incorrectly.
walkthrough: For [1,3,5], n is 5 and the missing pair is 2,4. The combined XOR is 6 (binary 110); choosing its low set bit 2 separates 2 from 4. Present numbers cancel in each bit group, leaving those two values, returned as [2,4].
edgeCases: Empty input, missing endpoints, arbitrary input order.
The largest n; arithmetic square-sum formulas would exceed ordinary int bounds.

explanation: Keep the tallest barrier seen from each end. The side with the lower established barrier can be settled now: the opposite barrier is already high enough to support that level. If the current bar raises its own barrier, it holds no water; otherwise its deficit is final. Move inward without allocating prefix/suffix arrays.
timeComplexity: O(n) time: one pointer moves inward per iteration.
spaceComplexity: O(1) auxiliary scalar storage; no height-sized or input-sized arrays.
attribution: Independently authored EPI Practice description, examples, implementation and explanation. Exercise reference: Cracking the Coding Interview, sixth edition, 17.21. No affiliation is implied.
correctness: All positions outside the two pointers have been settled correctly. The two maxima record barriers already encountered on each side. If the left maximum is no greater than the right maximum, a left bar below that left maximum has exactly that water level: a left barrier establishes it, and the right barrier is high enough. A taller left bar raises the maximum and holds zero water. The symmetric argument settles a right position when the right maximum is smaller. Each step settles one position and preserves the invariant, so the accumulated deficits give the complete volume when the pointers cross.
walkthrough: For [3,0,2,0,4], the water above positions is [0,3,1,3,0], totaling 7. The interior height-2 bar reduces water at its own position by two units; using just the distance and end heights would overcount.
edgeCases: Empty, short, monotone and all-zero histograms.
Several basins, equal end barriers, interior peaks, and maximum bounded volume.

A taller left bar raises the maximum and holds zero water. The symmetric argument settles a right position when the right maximum is smaller. Each step settles one position and preserves the invariant, so the accumulated deficits give the complete volume when the pointers cross.

explanation: Keep the tallest barrier seen from each end. The side with the lower established barrier can be settled now: the opposite barrier is already high enough to support that level. If the current bar raises its own barrier, it holds no water; otherwise its deficit is final. Move inward without allocating prefix/suffix arrays.
timeComplexity: O(n) time: one pointer moves inward per iteration.
spaceComplexity: O(1) auxiliary scalar storage; no height-sized or input-sized arrays.

explanation: Treat words as graph vertices and one-letter changes as edges. Breadth-first search discovers each word once and stores the predecessor that first reached it. Generate possible neighbors by changing one position to each other letter and checking dictionary membership, avoiding a comparison against every word for every step.
timeComplexity: Expected O(D+26*W*L^2) character work for D dictionary characters, W reachable length-L words and copying/hashing each generated length-L candidate. At most 26*L candidates are tried per expanded word.
spaceComplexity: O(D+W*L) dictionary, visited/predecessor/queue and returned-word storage.
attribution: Independently authored EPI Practice description, examples, implementation and explanation. Exercise reference: Cracking the Coding Interview, sixth edition, 17.22. No affiliation is implied.
correctness: Every generated neighbor changes exactly one position and is queued only if it is a dictionary word, so every predecessor edge is a legal transformation. Visited tracking prevents repeated vertices and guarantees finite exploration. Induction on path length shows BFS discovers every reachable word; thus queue exhaustion proves no path exists. When stop is found, following predecessors back to start and reversing yields a valid path with both endpoints and no repeated word. The identical-endpoint case is the one-word path.
walkthrough: With dictionary=[cat,cot,cog,dog], start cat changes a to o to reach cot, then t to g to reach cog, then c to d to reach dog. Return [cat,cot,cog,dog]. cat->dog directly is invalid because several positions differ.
edgeCases: Equal endpoints, disconnected components and direct one-letter neighbors.
Repeated dictionary entries, other word lengths, cycles and several valid paths.

explanation: Precompute how many consecutive black cells begin at each position going right and down. Four run-length checks then verify any candidate border in constant time. Search side lengths from largest to smallest and top-left positions in row order so the first valid candidate also satisfies the tie rule.
timeComplexity: O(n^3) time: O(n^2) preprocessing and O(n^3) candidates with four constant-time border checks.
spaceComplexity: O(n^2) auxiliary right/down run-length tables.
attribution: Independently authored EPI Practice description, examples, implementation and explanation. Exercise reference: Cracking the Coding Interview, sixth edition, 17.23. No affiliation is implied.
correctness: Processing cells from bottom-right computes exact right/down black-run lengths: a white cell has zero, while a black cell extends the adjacent run by one. A candidate of side s has an all-black border exactly when its top and bottom horizontal runs and left and right vertical runs each reach s. Interior values do not enter these checks. Descending sizes guarantee maximality of the first valid result; row/column order guarantees the requested earliest top-left tie. If no candidate succeeds, no side-one black cell exists either, so [] is correct.
walkthrough: For [[0,0,0],[0,1,0],[0,0,0]], all four length-three edges are black even though the center is white, so return [0,0,3]. Requiring a completely filled black square would incorrectly reject the correct answer.
edgeCases: Empty and all-white input; one black cell.
A hollow black border, a broken edge with black corners, and tied largest squares.
