explanation: Fix top and bottom rows and add their strip into one column-sum array. Any rectangle with those row bounds becomes a contiguous subarray of column sums. A nonempty Kadane scan finds the best such column interval in linear time. Extending the bottom row incrementally reuses column totals instead of resumming each rectangle.
timeComplexity: O(rows^2*columns) time for all row pairs and their column scans.
spaceComplexity: O(columns) auxiliary column totals plus constant scalar bounds and the five-integer result.
attribution: Independently authored EPI Practice description, examples, implementation and explanation. Exercise reference: Cracking the Coding Interview, sixth edition, 17.24. No affiliation is implied.
correctness: For each row pair, each column total is exactly the sum between those rows. Therefore a column interval and its corresponding rectangle have identical sums. Kadane keeps the maximum nonempty sum ending at each column: extend a nonnegative preceding sum, or start anew after a negative one. Every possible rectangle has one enumerated row pair and column interval, so maximizing these candidates yields the global optimum. Keeping an equal-zero prefix favors earlier left bounds; strict global improvements with top/bottom iteration order preserve the specified tie priority. Initializing below all admitted sums prevents an empty zero choice from defeating all-negative rectangles.
walkthrough: For [[1,-2,3],[-4,5,6]], the bottom row interval columns 1..2 sums to 11. Including both rows over those columns gives -2+3+5+6=12, so return [12,0,1,1,2]. In [[-5,-2]], the correct nonempty answer is [-2,0,1,0,1], not zero.
edgeCases: Empty dimensions, a single negative cell, all-negative matrices.
The entire matrix, a strict interior optimum, and ties under the stated top/bottom/left/right priority.

explanation: Try height/width pairs from largest area downward. For a fixed pair, append candidate row words and check whether every partial column is still a prefix of some dictionary word of the required column height. An impossible prefix can never be repaired by later rows, so pruning avoids exploring the rest of that branch.
timeComplexity: Exponential search in the maximum word length L: O(D^L*(L+1)^4) conservative character work for at most D distinct dictionary words across O(L^2) dimension pairs, including copying/hashing column prefixes. L<=5 bounds this search; pruning can greatly reduce it.
spaceComplexity: O(D*(L+1)^2) dictionary/prefix characters plus O(L^2) candidate/result grid and O(L) recursion frames.
attribution: Independently authored EPI Practice description, examples, implementation and explanation. Exercise reference: Cracking the Coding Interview, sixth edition, 17.25. No affiliation is implied.
correctness: Every completed accepted row sequence uses dictionary row words and has each full column in the required-height dictionary group, so it is a valid rectangle. At a partial state, a column prefix absent from every possible full column word cannot extend to any valid solution; rejecting it is safe. Trying every candidate row at each unpruned depth therefore finds a rectangle for those dimensions whenever one exists. Dimensions are considered in decreasing area, so the first successful rectangle has globally maximum area. Exhaustion proves no nonempty rectangle exists.
walkthrough: For words=[ab,ba], rows [ab,ba] make columns ab and ba, giving area 4. Rows [ba,ab] are another accepted maximum. With words=[aa], reusing aa twice gives [aa,aa], whose columns are also aa. With only [ab], no compatible column words exist, so return [].
edgeCases: Empty vocabulary, no compatible rectangle, one-letter words and nonsquare maxima.
Reused words, duplicate entries, equal-area alternate rectangles and column-prefix dead ends.

correctness: Every completed accepted row sequence uses dictionary row words and has each full column in the required-height dictionary group, so it is a valid rectangle. At a partial state, a column prefix absent from every possible full column word cannot extend to any valid solution; rejecting it is safe. Trying every candidate row at each unpruned depth therefore finds a rectangle for those dimensions whenever one exists. Dimensions are considered in decreasing area, so the first successful rectangle has globally maximum area. Exhaustion proves no nonempty rectangle exists.
walkthrough: For words=[ab,ba], rows [ab,ba] make columns ab and ba, giving area 4. Rows [ba,ab] are another accepted maximum. With words=[aa], reusing aa twice gives [aa,aa], whose columns are also aa. With only [ab], no compatible column words exist, so return [].
edgeCases: Empty vocabulary, no compatible rectangle, one-letter words and nonsquare maxima.

explanation: Most document pairs may share nothing. Build an inverted index from each word ID to the document positions containing it. A pair appears together once for each shared word, so incrementing only those pairs computes positive intersection sizes without testing every disjoint pair. Document lengths then give union=lengthA+lengthB-intersection. C# Dictionary counters use the sparse key i*n+j for document positions i<j. This is a unique address below n*n, not a dense matrix allocation. Output maps through documentIds and uses CompareTo for ordering, avoiding overflow from subtracting arbitrary signed IDs.
timeComplexity: Expected O(T+sum(f_w^2)+P log(P+1)) time for T word occurrences, posting frequency f_w per word and P positive document pairs. Posting-pair work can still be quadratic when many documents share words.
spaceComplexity: O(T+P+n) inverted postings, sparse intersection counters and result rows for n documents; no dense n-by-n matrix is allocated.
attribution: Independently authored EPI Practice description, examples, implementation and explanation. Exercise reference: Cracking the Coding Interview, sixth edition, 17.26. No affiliation is implied.
correctness: Because each document contains a word ID at most once, a word posting list contributes exactly one increment to each pair sharing that word. Summing over words therefore yields the exact intersection count for every recorded pair, and records no zero-intersection pair. Inclusion-exclusion gives its exact union size. Mapping positions back to the supplied unique document IDs, normalizing pair orientation and sorting yields each required row once. Empty documents appear in no posting list and correctly contribute no positive pair.
walkthrough: For IDs [10,20,30] and documents [[1,2],[2,3],[]], word 2 links documents 10 and 20 once. Their intersection is 1 and union is 2+2-1=3, so return [[10,20,1,3]], representing exact similarity 1/3. Empty document 30 creates no positive pair.
edgeCases: No documents, empty/disjoint documents and identical sets.
Arbitrary/signed-endpoint document IDs, input order differing from ID order and several shared words.
Word duplicates inside one document are outside the set-input domain.
